origin: Recorded at Fondi and in the Pontine area; identification with ancient Caecuban grapes is only a historical hypothesis.
summary: Historic Lazio red capable of structured wines and ageing.
viticulture: Moderate vigour and variable moderate crops; exposed foothills, short pruning.
winemaking: Red vinification; ageing is possible although colour can decline.
taste: Amaranth red, full-bodied and structured.
confusions: Ancient Cecubo references cannot prove the identity of modern Abbuoto.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage not established in the sources reviewed.

summary: A vigorous white breeding selection with comparatively neutral wines.
origin: Obtained by Wanner and cultivated in eastern France.
viticulture: Fertile under short pruning; early budbreak exposes it to spring frost. Sensitive to grey rot. Large bunches and medium-to-large berries.
winemaking: White-wine production; clone 1376 is recorded.
taste: Neutral rather than strongly aromatic.
geneticsNote: Montpellier analysis reported by Plantgrape supports Madeleine Royale × Kövidinka.
confusions: Do not merge Abondant with Abondance solely because both names evoke productivity.

summary: Early-ripening Southwest red with substantial colour and tannin.
origin: Probably from around Villeréal, Lot-et-Garonne; reported by Numa Naugé in the late nineteenth century.
viticulture: Moderate vigour, good fertility and short-pruning suitability. Generally little disease susceptibility, including relatively good grey-rot tolerance. Vassal: budbreak +1 day, maturity +1 week versus Chasselas.
winemaking: Used in Côtes-du-Marmandais red and rosé blends; low acidity is a significant blending consideration.
taste: Deep colour, full body, firm tannin and relatively low acidity.
confusions: Early ripening should not be mistaken for intrinsically light structure.
geneticsNote: The cited profile does not establish complete parentage.

summary: Known for vivid red fruit and relatively supple tannins, but capable of more than an easy-drinking style. Low yields, ripe fruit and maturation can produce substantial dry reds.
origin: Nemea, in the Greek Peloponnese, is its principal reference region.
viticulture: Nemea’s differing elevations and climatic zones produce a range of ripeness levels; harvest timing and yield management help determine the intended style.
winemaking: Young dry reds, oak-matured wines, rosé and sweet wines from sun-dried grapes are all made. The use of an appellation on the label must be assessed for the particular wine category.
taste: Cherry, plum and sweet spices. Young wines often have moderate acidity and supple tannins; selected cuvées are more concentrated.
geneticsNote: The complete parentage has not been verified in this edition; hypotheses are not presented as established findings.
confusions: St. George is a translation of the name, not proof that every wine bearing that name worldwide is made from this variety.

summary: One of southern Italy’s most structured red varieties. Acidity, tannin and a long ripening cycle underpin its ageing potential. Taurasi, Taburno and Vulture merit separate comparison.
origin: Southern Italy, with strong associations with Campania and Basilicata. The traditional account of a Greek origin is not a confirmed genetic origin.
viticulture: Early budding and late ripening; requires a sufficiently long warm season. Grey rot and sour rot require attention in wet autumns.
winemaking: Suited to dry reds and extended maturation. Extraction and oak ageing need to reflect tannin ripeness; earlier-drinking styles also exist.
taste: Black cherry, wild berries and spice. Usually high in acidity and tannin; leather and earthy notes can develop with age.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage has not been verified for this entry. Similar names and local origin stories are not treated as evidence of genetic relationships.
confusions: Aglianicone is a separate variety. The name Aglianico alone does not prove direct introduction from ancient Greece.

summary: Long associated with extensive plantings and distillation base wine, Airén can also produce fresh still whites. Old vines, controlled yields and precise winemaking can yield more distinctive expressions.

taste: Relatively neutral, with apple, light citrus and white flowers. Structure depends on yield and ripeness.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage was not verified in the regional and producer sources reviewed for this entry. This does not imply that no scientific research exists.
confusions: Large planted area does not make every wine low quality, and distillation base wine is not its only use.

origin: Long established in the Romagna hills of Emilia-Romagna, with Bertinoro an important centre. Stories of Roman introduction are not established genetic history.
summary: A structured Romagna white grape used for dry, sweet and passito wines; phenolic grip is particularly relevant in dry examples.
viticulture: Late budbreak; intermediate ripening. Vigorous, reliably productive; elongated bunches with amber berries. Long pruning and canopy management are customary. Favours sunny, dry hillsides; avoid waterlogged, chlorosis-prone soils. Some powdery-mildew susceptibility.
winemaking: Dry wines may retain phenolic structure; grape drying concentrates passito. Romagna Albana DOCG encompasses secco, amabile, dolce, passito and passito riserva.
taste: Floral and fruity, with substantial body and sometimes light tannic grip when dry. Sweetness, concentration and golden-to-amber colour vary with processing.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage has not been verified in the sources consulted for this record.
confusions: Dry and sweet Albana are wine styles of the same grape; a golden colour does not establish botrytis treatment.

summary: A rare southeastern Sicilian white with both dry and sweet traditions.
origin: Siracusa is the historic centre, with surviving vines also in Ragusa; described by Nicosia in 1735.

confusions: Not Albanella from Marche; historical Montonico Bianco applied to Albanello in eastern Sicily is a misnaming.

origin: Documented in the Tuscan historical tradition since the Middle Ages; Elba, Lazio and Puglia are important centres. Its ultimate place of origin is not securely established.
summary: An aromatic black grape with muscat, rose and berry character, especially associated with sweet and dried-grape wines.
viticulture: Generally mid-season budbreak; ripening varies by site and clone. Moderate vigour and crop; berries have a clear muscat flavour. Choose dry, ventilated sites. Cold, wet springs can cause poor set and shot berries; sound fruit is essential before drying.
winemaking: May be vinified from fresh grapes or after appassimento on the vine or in ventilated spaces. Sugar, alcohol and ageing depend on the specific wine.
taste: Rose, violet, berries and ripe cherry; drying and ageing can add jam and dried-fruit notes. Aromatic character does not by itself imply sweetness.
geneticsNote: Italian Vitis Database reports a proposed natural cross involving Moscato Bianco and an unidentified variety. The complete pedigree is unverified; this remains a hypothesis.
confusions: Not a black colour mutation of Moscato: research supports Muscat kinship and seedling origin. Pelaverde is a verified synonym, not Pelaverga Grosso or Pelaverga Piccolo.

taste: Dark fruit, plum and spice; very deep colour and substantial structure, with style dependent on site and harvest.
geneticsNote: A deliberate crossing by the Bouschet family in France: Petit Bouschet × Garnacha Tinta. Petit Bouschet itself derives from Aramon × Teinturier.
confusions: Not ordinary Garnacha and not an interspecific hybrid: both parents are Vitis vinifera.

summary: A historic high-yield Languedoc black grape, now of heritage interest.
origin: Native to Languedoc; once a major productive regional variety.
viticulture: At Vassal, buds two days before Chasselas and ripens about 4½ weeks later. Fertile, weak-growing and drooping: prune short. Sunburn, mites, downy mildew and phomopsis are concerns.
winemaking: Large clusters and very large berries; low sugar accumulation and modest colour make yield control central to wine concentration.
taste: Usually pale and lightly distinguished in the technical trials; this does not describe every modern low-yield bottling.
geneticsNote: Published genetics suggest Gouais Blanc × Ouliven; Plantgrape qualifies this as probable.
confusions: Aramon Blanc and Aramon Gris are separately recorded colour mutations.

summary: A rare white Aramon mutation with very high fertility.
origin: White-fruited mutation of Aramon, preserved in Aude.

winemaking: Very large clusters and berries. The technical record reports simple white wine rather than a concentrated aromatic style.
taste: Reported trial wines lack lift and finesse; no specific fruit aromas are documented.
geneticsNote: A white berry-colour mutation of Aramon.
confusions: White mutation, not a synonym of the black Aramon record.

summary: A French white cross capable of retaining acid alongside high sugar.
origin: Bred by INRA in 1961.
viticulture: Upright and fairly fertile; short pruning and gobelet are possible. Very low grey-rot sensitivity. Budburst +5 days, maturity +2½ weeks versus Chasselas.
winemaking: Small berries on large clusters combine high sugar and acid potential. Overripe harvests can produce sweet wine.
taste: Balanced alcohol and acidity with worthwhile aromatic potential; the source does not specify individual fruit notes.

summary: One of the rare traditional white varieties of Champagne. Low yields and a long ripening cycle help explain its limited commercial expansion.
origin: Northeastern France, probably the Aube.
viticulture: Early budding and relatively late ripening; northern sites require warmth and favourable exposure. Very low yielding and susceptible to disease, especially downy mildew.
winemaking: Used in traditional-method sparkling wine, including varietal Champagne. Good sugar accumulation together with retained acidity can provide a fine structure.
taste: Usually lively in acidity and delicate aromatically. Comité Champagne mentions hawthorn, carnation, peach, apple and quince; aromatic intensity remains dependent on site and winemaking.
geneticsNote: The official sources used for this entry do not establish both parents. Co-planting with other Champagne varieties is not evidence of kinship.
confusions: Arbane is distinct from Arneis and Alban. Traditional rare Champagne varieties and current experimental-variety rules require separate verification.

summary: An early red selected for light, fruit-led drinking.

summary: An important Central European red variety combining high acidity and spice. Fine examples offer dark fruit, tannic structure and distinct site expression; Austrian reds are not uniformly light or simple.

summary: A distinct selection from the Bouquet resistance-breeding programme.

origin: Piedmont, especially Asti and Alessandria between the Belbo and Bormida rivers, with Acqui a key reference.
summary: A rose-scented aromatic red grape, best known for sweet frizzante and sparkling wines, with dry and rosé expressions also represented.
viticulture: Early budbreak and early ripening in Piedmont. Moderate vigour and restrained, regular crops; aromatic berries in small-to-medium bunches. Virus health, especially leafroll, can constrain spring growth. Early ripening often reduces exposure to late bunch rots.
winemaking: Used for sweet frizzante, spumante and passito; the modern Acqui range also includes dry and rosé wines, beyond the familiar low-alcohol sweet style.
taste: Rose is a key aromatic marker; ruby colour and pronounced perfume. Residual sugar and bubbles are wine-style variables.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage has not been verified in the sources consulted for this record.
confusions: Brachetto di Roero, Brachetto Migliardi and the similarly named French Braquet must not automatically be equated with this cultivar.

summary: Known for dark fruit, pronounced tannins and ageing capacity, Cabernet Sauvignon supplies much of the structure of Bordeaux Left Bank wines. Depending on temperature, its expression ranges from blackcurrant, cedar and herbs to riper blackberry fruit.
origin: Bordeaux, France.
viticulture: Late budding and late ripening, with small berries and thick skins. Requires sufficient warmth and well-drained sites; herbal notes are more prominent with incomplete ripeness.
winemaking: Often blended with Merlot and Cabernet Franc, but also made as a varietal wine. Maceration, extraction and oak ageing should be matched to fruit maturity.
taste: Blackcurrant and blackberry, sometimes bell pepper and mint. Usually medium-high to high tannin with evident acidity; cedar and tobacco are commonly associated with maturation.
geneticsNote: DNA research establishes the parents. A natural crossing, not a modern deliberately bred cross.
confusions: Cabernet Franc is one parent, not the same variety. Bell-pepper character in Cabernet Sauvignon cannot always be attributed entirely to unripe fruit.

summary: An Italian resistant selection registered in France under its UD breeding code.
origin: University of Udine–IGA breeding, developed with VCR; French classification in 2022.
viticulture: Medium budbreak and ripening in VCR trials. Moderate vigour, semi-upright; fertile basal buds suit short pruning. Good downy-mildew resistance, moderate powdery resistance; black rot and Phomopsis need protection.
winemaking: High sugar, good fixed acidity and phenolics suit medium–long ageing.
taste: Intense fruity expression recalling Cabernet Sauvignon.
geneticsNote: Direct cross given by the breeder; the UD code and commercial name identify the same variety.
confusions: A distinct bred variety, not a clone of its familiar vinifera parent.

origin: An INRA crossing from the 1970s, registered in France in 2014.
summary: An INRA crossing from the 1970s, registered in France in 2014. Moderate alcohol potential, retained acidity, stable colour and relatively supple tannins; spice, cocoa and red fruit.
viticulture: Moderate, regular production; sensitive to magnesium deficiency and leafhoppers. No marked mildew or grey-rot susceptibility is reported.
winemaking: Small to medium berries in relatively loose bunches; suitable for red or rosé vinification.
taste: Moderate alcohol potential, retained acidity, stable colour and relatively supple tannins; spice, cocoa and red fruit.

summary: A newly catalogued Savoie heritage white retaining acidity alongside good sugar potential.
origin: Native to Savoie; Plantgrape records French listing and classification in 2026.
viticulture: Low to moderate vigour, semi-upright to upright and moderately productive. Compact bunches with thin-skinned berries make grey rot a concern; no special mildew susceptibility is reported. Vassal: buds with Chasselas, ripens two weeks later.
winemaking: Potential for fresh dry whites; reasonably high sugar accumulation is balanced by retained acidity. No established barrel-ageing regime is prescribed.
taste: Lively and aromatically restrained rather than demonstrably Muscat-like or intensely perfumed.
geneticsNote: The Hibou Noir profile suggests a relationship with Cacaboué, but a parent pair is not established.
confusions: The B suffix in the French catalogue denotes white berry colour and is not part of the variety’s name.

summary: Galician white grape offering high acidity, aromatic intensity and body; used alone and to complement Albariño in Rías Baixas.
origin: Associated with Galicia. Historical references to an unspecified Caíño cannot always distinguish white from red cultivars.
viticulture: EVEGA records early-to-mid budburst and medium-late ripening near Albariño. Moderate yields; downy mildew is a major susceptibility, with lesser powdery-mildew and Botrytis sensitivity.
winemaking: Fresh varietal whites and blends; barrel and bottle maturation are both possible. Its acid structure can complement softer components.
taste: High acidity and body with apple, other pip-fruit and floral notes. Reported analytical figures from trials should not be read as universal specifications.
confusions: Not Albariño, Savagnin Blanc or a simple colour form of Caíño Tinto; molecular and ampelographic work establishes separate identity.

summary: Northwestern Iberian red grape valued for acidity and tannic structure. Borraçal is an important Portuguese name; Ribeiro and Rías Baixas are Spanish references.
origin: Long cultivated in Galicia and northern Portugal; the reviewed evidence does not securely locate the original seedling on one side of the border.
viticulture: Late ripening, with budburst classified differently by EVEGA and VCR. Vigorous with low bud fertility; longer pruning can help. Small, moderately compact bunches.
winemaking: Usually a red-wine component contributing acidity and structure; extraction should reflect its potentially firm, astringent tannin.
taste: High acidity with substantial tannin; vegetal or herbal notes can accompany the fruit. Maturity and extraction strongly affect balance.
confusions: Several distinct Caíño genotypes exist. EVEGA also records Caíño Redondo as a Ribeiro local name for Caíño Tinto: the same name can refer to different accessions, so geographic and genetic context matter.

summary: Mallorca red grape central to Pla i Llevant, often producing moderately alcoholic, lightly coloured wines with a distinctive red-fruit and floral expression.
origin: Established in eastern Mallorca, especially around Felanitx and Manacor; historical references appear in the late nineteenth century.
viticulture: Vigorous and productive. Fertile soils can prolong growth and impair ripening and colour; poorer sites help restrain vigour. Regional descriptions classify budburst and ripening as medium-early.
winemaking: Varietal reds and blends; ÀN/2 is a documented Callet-led blend. White vinification also occurs, so berry colour does not dictate the finished wine.
taste: Typically modest colour and medium alcohol; red fruit, rose or violet can appear. Oak-derived flavours should be separated from the grape profile.
confusions: Callet is distinct from Callet Negrella, its reported parent formerly called Callet Cas Concos, and from Manto Negro.

summary: The white Carignan mutation, late ripening and sensitive to powdery mildew.
origin: White mutation of Carignan.
viticulture: High, regular fertility supports short pruning. Particularly vulnerable to powdery mildew. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +10 days; maturity +4½ weeks.

taste: The baseline technical profile is relatively neutral, with comparatively high alcohol.
geneticsNote: A white berry-colour mutation of Carignan.
confusions: Distinct from Carignan Gris and from white wine pressed from black Carignan.

summary: A very late Carignan mutation whose drought adaptation and bitterness require careful management.
origin: Grey mutation of Carignan; entered the French catalogue in 2017.
viticulture: Upright, wind-resistant and suited to poor, dry soils; short-prune as gobelet or cordon. Very powdery-mildew sensitive. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +12 days, maturity +6 weeks.
winemaking: Very late ripening requires site selection. Compact medium clusters; substantial alcohol potential can be accompanied by bitterness.
taste: Aromatics vary strongly by site; avoid assigning one fixed fruit signature.
geneticsNote: A grey berry-colour mutation of Carignan.
confusions: A true grey mutation, not Carignan Blanc or a blanc de noirs from Carignan.

summary: Historically part of the Bordeaux varietal repertoire, Carmenère subsequently developed a distinctive identity in Chile. Ripe dark fruit, spice and herbal notes form a recognisable combination.
origin: Bordeaux, France; Chile now has the most representative commercial plantings.
viticulture: Late ripening, with irregular flowering and fruit set. Requires a sufficiently long, warm ripening season. Vigour and shade management affect pyrazine-related bell-pepper character.
winemaking: Made as a varietal wine or blended with Cabernet Sauvignon and other varieties. Harvest ripeness and measured extraction matter more than concentration alone.
taste: Blackberry, plum, sweet pepper, pepper and spice. Ripe examples often have a supple texture while retaining clear herbal notes.
geneticsNote: UC Davis FPS lists Cabernet Franc × Gros Cabernet as likely parentage; its Bordeaux chapter also gives this pairing. The qualification attached to the evidence is retained.
confusions: Distinct from Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Herbal character varies in intensity and cannot alone determine a blind-tasting conclusion.

summary: A principal variety of Etna Bianco, known for marked acidity, delicate aromas and ageing potential. The eastern slopes and higher-elevation sites are important points of reference.
origin: A traditional white variety of Etna, Sicilia, Italy.
viticulture: Locally often trained as alberello. Mid- to late-season ripening; cooler conditions and diurnal temperature variation favour delicate expression.
winemaking: Made as a varietal wine or blended with varieties such as Catarratto. Stainless steel, lees ageing and judicious oak ageing are all used.
taste: Citrus blossom, white-fleshed fruit and taut acidity. Greater textural depth can develop with age; “minerality” is a sensory description.
geneticsNote: A 2021 SNP study confirmed this parental combination and revised earlier accounts.
confusions: Carricante and Catarratto are distinct varieties. A volcanic origin does not establish grape identity.

summary: An important Sicilian white variety. Catarratto Bianco Comune and Catarratto Bianco Lucido have separate entries in the Italian national register, although research has found matching microsatellite (SSR) profiles. This entry groups them under Catarratto while retaining their distinct registrations and morphological differences.
origin: A longstanding white variety of Sicilia, Italy.
viticulture: Vigorous. Comune and Lucido vine material differ in bunch characteristics and ripening behaviour; fruit health requires attention in damp conditions.
winemaking: Commonly used for dry whites and blends, with some skin-contact expressions. Historically used in Marsala base wines.
taste: Citrus, herbs, white-fleshed fruit and moderate structure, sometimes with slight bitterness.
geneticsNote: Comune, Lucido and extra-lucido material share SSR profiles in published research and are considered morphological variation within the variety. Matching marker profiles do not demonstrate identity at every genetic locus or mean that all material constitutes a single clone. Complete parentage has not been verified for this entry.
confusions: This is a consolidated library entry, not grounds for removing the separate registered identities of Comune and Lucido or specific clone information. They differ in bloom, bunch characteristics and other phenotypic traits. Carricante is another variety, not a synonym.

aliases.name: Catarratto Bianco Comune
aliases.context: A separately registered name in the Italian national catalogue. Included here alongside Catarratto material with the same SSR profile, without erasing its registered identity.

aliases.name: Catarratto Bianco Lucido
aliases.context: Another separately registered name in the Italian national catalogue. Differs from Comune in bloom and other morphological and viticultural traits, despite an identical SSR profile.

aliases.name: Lucido

summary: A vigorous, pink-skinned Argentine criolla with a major role in wine and must production; distinct from both Criolla Grande and Criolla Chica.
origin: An Argentine natural crossing, traditionally grown in Cuyo and frequently interplanted with Criolla Grande.
viticulture: Very productive and tolerant of saline soils. Very large, loose bunches with large obovoid berries. Downy mildew and berry splitting followed by rot are important hazards.
winemaking: Much production enters blended wines or must; large berries also give table-grape potential, although that is not its principal Argentine role.
taste: The reviewed official sources do not support a precise universal aroma profile. Pink skin is not evidence that every resulting wine is rosé.
confusions: Cereza means cherry in Spanish, but the name is not a tasting descriptor. It is not a synonym of Criolla Grande.

summary: An interspecific red wine grape used for varietal wines and blends; Missouri is a useful reference.
origin: A French-American hybrid with documented cultivation in France and Missouri.
viticulture: Vigorous; tolerates winter cold but is sensitive to drought and chlorosis. Reduced mildew susceptibility does not mean immunity; phylloxera remains a risk.
winemaking: Can contribute colour to red blends. Oak treatment and residual sugar must be checked in the individual wine.
taste: Missouri references show cherry, darker cherry and earthy notes, medium body and relatively supple tannin. Oak aromas reflect élevage.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape reports genetic support for 11369 Joannès Seyve × Plantet (5455 Seibel). This is interspecific ancestry, not pure vinifera.
confusions: Do not confuse this red variety with the white hybrid Chardonel.

summary: A white variety that clearly expresses climate, site and winemaking choices. Styles range from lean and citrus-led to ripe and full-bodied; it is also fundamental to traditional-method sparkling wine.
origin: Burgundy, France.
viticulture: Early budding, with significant spring-frost risk. Widely adaptable but capable of high yields. Harvest timing determines the balance of acidity, sugar and flavour.
winemaking: Stainless steel, oak, malolactic fermentation and lees stirring are all possible, but none is obligatory. Still whites and Blanc de Blancs sparkling wines are common.
taste: Cool sites often give lemon and green apple; warmer sites can produce peach and tropical fruit. Butter character arises through winemaking, while vanilla and toast commonly come from oak.
geneticsNote: DNA research supports a natural crossing between the Pinot family and Gouais Blanc. A Pinot colour form is not specified where the cited source does not distinguish one.
confusions: Chardonnay is distinct from Pinot Blanc. Butter is not an obligatory, inherent varietal aroma.

summary: The pink-skinned form of Chardonnay, broadly similar to white Chardonnay in cultivation and winemaking. It joined Champagne AOC’s principal authorised-variety list on 31 July 2025; actual plantings remain very small.
origin: A natural pink-skin mutation of Chardonnay, identified in Champagne and Burgundy by the early twentieth century. Discovery locations do not establish a single site of mutation.
viticulture: Small, compact bunches and small to medium berries. Pl@ntGrape observes slightly later ripening and slightly lower yields than white Chardonnay, broadly similar disease susceptibility and possibly slightly lower susceptibility to grey rot. These comparisons are not fixed differences at every site.
winemaking: Can be used in Champagne base wines and blends, with choices broadly comparable to Chardonnay. Pink skins do not necessarily produce rosé; ripeness, pressing and acidity determine the wine style.
taste: Broadly similar to Chardonnay. Comité Champagne emphasises freshness and sometimes more pronounced fruit. Acidity comparisons vary by source and conditions: Pl@ntGrape reports slightly lower acidity, while the Champagne description mentions occasionally higher acidity. Neither is treated here as a fixed varietal rule.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape and Comité Champagne explicitly identify a natural pink-skin mutation of Chardonnay, not a cross between two varieties.
confusions: Distinct from Pinot Gris and from rosé wine names without a genetic meaning. Its principal authorised status in Champagne differs from Voltis’s adaptation-trial status.

winemaking: Large bunches. Acidity falls rapidly in warm conditions; cooler sites are preferable. Wines can oxidize readily.
taste: Aromatic white wines; freshness depends strongly on site and harvest timing.

summary: A fertile Grenache–Jurançon cross for warm, dry conditions.
origin: Bred by INRA in 1958.
viticulture: Highly fertile: short-prune and control crop, especially in young vines. Adapted to hot, dry sites and gobelet; stem desiccation can occur, notably on SO4. Low grey-rot sensitivity. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +6 days; maturity +2½–3 weeks.
winemaking: Large bunches and small berries; crop balance underpins quality.
taste: Supple, fruity and generous wines with distinct character.
geneticsNote: INRA bred this cross in 1958: Garnacha Tinta × Jurançon Noir.
confusions: Ganson shares the same stated parents but is a separate selection.

summary: High acidity and versatility support excellent bone-dry, sparkling and botrytised sweet wines. South African old-vine dry whites and the Loire Valley’s range of sweetness levels are important comparative references.
origin: The Loire Valley, France, particularly Anjou.
viticulture: Relatively early budding, requiring attention to spring frost. Uneven ripening and noble-rot development can require successive picking passes. Yield management strongly affects concentration.
winemaking: Suitable for stainless steel, barrel fermentation or maturation, lees ageing and traditional-method sparkling production. Residual sugar must be assessed wine by wine. High acidity supports sweet wines and long ageing.
taste: Green apple, quince, pear and beeswax; ripe or botrytised examples may show honey and apricot. Relatively high acidity is a characteristic structural feature.
geneticsNote: UC Davis FPS cites DNA research identifying Savagnin Blanc as one parent. The other parent is not established in this entry, so a complete crossing is not presented.
confusions: Chenin Blanc is distinct from Sauvignon Blanc. The word Pineau in Pineau de la Loire does not mean Pinot.

summary: A black-berried American hybrid significant in early European direct-producer and rootstock history. Historic; excluded from EU wine-grape classification under Article 81.
origin: A nineteenth-century American cultivar disseminated from New York by the 1830s. Hedrick records conflicting origin stories and a possible relationship to the older Worthington name, so an exact discovery narrative is not treated as settled.
viticulture: Historical New York observations describe very vigorous, spreading growth, early flowering and late edible maturity despite early colour. Spring frost, excessive growth and sensitivity to lime-rich soils were practical limitations. Cuttings rooted readily, and phylloxera resistance made it attractive in nineteenth-century France.
winemaking: Hedrick records French plantings and wine use, but found the wine harsh when young, with some softening in age. This is a historical appraisal, not a contemporary producer tasting or a universal quality judgment.
taste: Historical fresh-fruit observations emphasize acidity, a small berry and noticeable skin and seed contribution; these are not a standard modern wine tasting profile.
geneticsNote: Historically described as a riparia–labrusca hybrid. No named cultivar parents are securely assigned here. Its role as a parent in other crosses does not establish its own pedigree.
confusions: Clinton and Isabella are distinct. Worthington is retained as a historical identity question rather than added as an unqualified synonym.

origin: Long cultivated in northwestern Italy, now centred on Oltrepò Pavese with plantings in Piedmont and Piacenza. Earlier origins remain uncertain.

winemaking: Blended with Barbera or Uva Rara and also bottled alone; styles include youthful still or frizzante wines and concentrated versions for longer ageing.

confusions: Bonarda in Oltrepò and some neighbouring districts commonly denotes Croatina, not Bonarda Piemontese or Uva Rara. Check place and actual composition.

summary: A German teinturier with pigmented flesh, valued for very deep colour in blends and occasional varietal wines.

summary: Known for intense colour and powerful tannins, Durif is more prominent in California and Australia than in its place of origin. Related to Syrah but a distinct variety.
origin: France; selected and propagated by François Durif in the nineteenth century.
viticulture: Moderate to relatively low vigour, with generally good fruit set. Heat-related shrivelling, winter cold injury, grey rot and black rot require attention. Full maturity does not necessarily mean overripeness.
winemaking: Used alone or to add colour and structure to blends. Extraction needs control; maturation can help integrate tannins.
taste: Blackberry, black plum, black pepper and concentrated fruit; usually deeply coloured, high in tannin and full-bodied.
geneticsNote: Genetic analysis establishes the parents. Durif historically selected and propagated a seedling; this should not automatically be described as a documented controlled-pollination cross.
confusions: Petite Sirah usually refers to Durif. Historical mixed plantings can contain other varieties, so not all old records can be mechanically merged.

summary: Texture and weight are often its main appeal. It can make varietal wines or add volume and structure to Mediterranean white blends.
origin: A white mutation of Garnacha, traditionally grown around the Mediterranean.
viticulture: Tolerates drought and wind and can suit poor, stony soils. Cooler sites and timely picking help retain acidity.
winemaking: Stainless steel, barrels and lees ageing are all used. Oxidation management and alcohol balance require attention.
taste: Pear, ripe white fruit, flowers and herbs; often a rounded palate, with acidity influenced by temperature and picking date.
geneticsNote: A colour mutation of Garnacha Tinta, not a crossing of two different parents.
confusions: Garnacha Blanca and Garnacha Gris should not be treated as one colour form.

summary: Red fruit, spice and supple texture are common features; high-altitude sites and old vines can give fine distinctions of place. Uses include dry reds, rosés, sparkling wines and naturally sweet wines.
origin: Generally attributed to Aragón, Spain; its historical spread is closely linked to the Mediterranean.

geneticsNote: Complete parentage was not verified in the regional and producer sources reviewed for this entry. This does not imply that no scientific research exists.
confusions: Garnacha Tintorera usually means Alicante Bouschet, not this variety. Grenache Blanc is a colour mutation.

taste: Relatively limited colour intensity.
geneticsNote: Historical interspecific cross reported by Plantgrape.
confusions: Garonnet and Villard Noir share parents but are separate selections.

summary: Rose and lychee aromas are often prominent, with broad texture and usually moderate acidity. Styles include dry wines, late-harvest wines and botrytised sweet wines.
origin: A pink-skinned, highly aromatic mutation within the Savagnin/Traminer family. Its name alone does not establish an origin in Tramin.
viticulture: Early budding, with spring-frost risk. Susceptible to coulure and often low yielding. Heat can make the aromatic profile heavy, so acidity and the harvest window deserve attention.
winemaking: Usually made to retain aromatic character; excessive new oak may obscure it. Residual sugar, botrytis and skin contact all alter palate expression.
taste: Rose, lychee, spice and orange peel; often full-bodied, with relatively high alcohol and medium-low acidity. A slight phenolic bitterness may appear on the finish.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape describes it as a pink-skinned, aromatic mutation of Savagnin Blanc.
confusions: Non-aromatic Traminer/Savagnin Rose material should not all be merged into Gewürztraminer. Intense aroma does not demonstrate residual sugar.

summary: A revived Lot red for fresh, light red and rosé wines.

winemaking: Suitable for reds and rosés intended for early drinking; the primary profile does not recommend long ageing.
taste: Fresh, light and floral, with low alcohol and limited anthocyanin.
geneticsNote: Montpellier analyses suggest Cot (Malbec) × Colombaud; the conclusion remains qualified in Plantgrape.
confusions: Despite a Malbec parentage hypothesis, it need not resemble a concentrated Cahors wine.

summary: An Austrian-bred white grape producing relatively neutral, substantial wines with useful extract.
origin: Bred by Fritz Zweigelt at Klosterneuburg in 1922; principally associated with Austrian cultivation.
viticulture: Late budburst and flowering; mid-season ripening, generally before Welschriesling. Short, dense bunches and round green-yellow berries; fertile, suited to short pruning and relatively adaptable to sites and soils. Susceptible to powdery mildew, with possible bunch-stem necrosis; comparatively good Botrytis tolerance and low splitting tendency.
winemaking: Suitable for dry and Prädikat whites. Potentially heavy cropping requires balancing yield and ripeness to preserve concentration and acidity.
taste: Usually less overtly aromatic; fullness, concentration and adequate acidity are more useful signatures.
geneticsNote: Welschriesling × Orangetraube, a deliberately bred crossing within Vitis vinifera.
confusions: Orangeriesling is a synonym, not evidence of Riesling parentage; Goldburger is not Goldmuskateller.

summary: The aromatic white known in Italy as Moscato Giallo, made into dry, sweet and sweet sparkling wines.
origin: Long associated with northeastern Italy. Klosterneuburg lists Italy as origin; earlier eastern-Mediterranean accounts remain hypotheses.
viticulture: Vigorous, loose-bunched and thick-skinned; needs warm, ventilated sites and crop management. Ripening is rated mid-early in Italian guidance but mid-late in Austria. Susceptible to excoriosis and iron/magnesium deficiency, with good Botrytis tolerance.
winemaking: Italian expressions include dry wines, dried-grape dessert wines and sweet sparkling wines; aromatic intensity varies by clone.
taste: Distinct Muscat aromatics, citrus and orange blossom; sweetness is a winemaking choice rather than a fixed varietal trait.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage is unconfirmed; Klosterneuburg describes a probable relationship as an offspring of Gelber Muskateller, not a proven complete pedigree.
confusions: Keep Moscato Giallo separate from Muscat Blanc à Petits Grains, called Gelber Muskateller in Austria and Germany; similar names do not justify merging.

summary: Its genetic importance far exceeds its present commercial planting. Historical natural crosses with the Pinot family produced important descendants including Chardonnay, Aligoté and Gamay.
origin: An ancient European variety of uncertain precise origin; research has proposed the western Balkans or central Europe.
viticulture: High and relatively consistent yields, with comparatively good winter cold tolerance. Millerandage can occur. Susceptible to fungal diseases, particularly grey rot, with thin skins and relatively compact bunches.
winemaking: Traditionally used for simple, high-acid, low-alcohol white wines. Modern small-scale conservation and revival wines require individual assessment.
taste: Official technical descriptions identify neutral aromas, relatively low alcohol and very high acidity. The quality of its descendants does not imply that it shares their flavours.
geneticsNote: Its own complete parentage is not confirmed in this entry; genetic research supports its role as a parent of numerous classic varieties.
confusions: Heunisch Weiss is a synonym. Pinot × Gouais denotes a family of natural crosses; the descendants are not clones of Gouais.

summary: A Southwest distilling grape with limited sugar accumulation.
origin: Associated with Southwest France; probably descended from Gouais Blanc.
viticulture: Productive, upright and suitable for short pruning; generates numerous laterals and suckers. Slight powdery-mildew susceptibility. Vassal: budbreak +6 days; late maturity around +4 weeks versus Chasselas.
winemaking: Its neutral, acidic base wines fit the distilling context; recorded among Armagnac grapes as Plant de Graisse.
taste: Neutral aromas, pronounced acidity and low sugar-derived alcohol potential.
confusions: Plant de Graisse is contextual Armagnac terminology, not proof of oily wine texture.

taste: Generous, moderately coloured wines with relatively little tannin.

confusions: Monerac has the same parents but is a separate selection.

summary: A nineteenth-century Bouschet teinturier with pigmented juice.

confusions: Grolleau Gris is a colour mutation. Grolleau is distinct from Gamay and is not one of the Cabernet varieties used for Cabernet d’Anjou.

summary: Austria’s signature white variety ranges from crisp, everyday wines to substantial, ageworthy single-vineyard expressions. White pepper is a useful clue, but ripeness and site often matter more than one aroma.
origin: Austria; its ancestry includes an old vine discovered at St. Georgen.
viticulture: Yield management governs concentration. Loess and weathered rock soils produce differing textures; a temperate climate with sufficient time to ripen is beneficial.
winemaking: Stainless steel, old wood and lees ageing are all common. Wines may be light or more extract-rich, full-bodied dry whites.
taste: Citrus, pear, apple, herbs and white pepper. Fine mature wines can develop honeyed, waxy and nutty complexity.
geneticsNote: Official Austrian sources identify Traminer and St. Georgen as parents.
confusions: Roter Veltliner is not its red version. The word Veltliner does not establish a shared ancestry among every variety bearing that name.

summary: A white variety documented by AGRIS in Sardegna as Granatza, with regular yields and relatively high grape acidity. The Guarnaccia name in Calabria covers genetically different material.
origin: AGRIS documents Granatza in old vineyards across Sardegna and identifies it with nationally registered Guarnaccia Bianca, code 106. The geographic origin is not settled by this synonymy.

winemaking: Traditionally associated with Sardinian dessert wines. AGRIS records historical confusion with Vernaccia di Oristano, although the genotypes differ.

(2021) found Guarnaccia Saracena/ARSAC distinct from the national-register and other database Guarnaccia profiles; do not apply this synonym to every Calabrian accession. Distinct from Vernaccia di Oristano.

summary: A rare Württemberg red and parent of Dornfelder, limited commercially by flowering sensitivity and variable crops.
origin: Bred by August Herold at Weinsberg in 1931 and registered in 1960; breeding designation We S 5332.
viticulture: Vigorous and relatively early, harvested shortly after Portugieser. Requires good sites and is lime-sensitive. Flowering sensitivity causes variable crops; nursery guidance reports comparatively low mildew susceptibility.
winemaking: Principally vinified as red wine, with delicate fruit rather than pronounced varietal perfume; oak regime cannot be inferred from the variety.
taste: Relatively neutral aromatics with delicate fruit; the darker profile of its offspring Dornfelder should not be assumed.
geneticsNote: Frühburgunder × Schiava Grossa (Trollinger); the breeder’s pedigree has genetic support.
confusions: Dornfelder is the offspring of Helfensteiner × Heroldrebe; the two parents are distinct cultivars.

summary: A black-berried hybrid whose historical French importance and pale-wine uses are easily missed when colour alone guides classification. Historic; excluded from EU wine-grape classification under Article 81.
origin: An old southeastern American grape associated with Nicholas Herbemont in Columbia, South Carolina. UC Davis records cultivation from the early nineteenth century, while Hedrick documents older traditions and conflicting origin stories.
viticulture: Historical accounts describe vigorous, productive vines requiring a long, warm season and well-drained soil. Cold sensitivity limited northern sites; chlorosis on calcareous soil, difficult propagation and only moderate phylloxera resistance restricted its value as a rootstock.
winemaking: UC Davis documents both white and light-red wines from its black berries, and current US collection material originating in Texas. It should not automatically be described as a deeply pigmented red-wine grape.
taste: Hedrick’s historical fruit description emphasizes tender, juicy flesh and sweet flavour; UC Davis records pale wine styles. These do not establish a cultivar-wide modern aroma list.
geneticsNote: UC Davis lists the traditional botanical designation Vitis bourquiniana and ancestry involving aestivalis, cinerea and vinifera. This is a species-level description, not a verified pair of named parents.
confusions: Herbemont is distinct from Jacquez/Lenoir. The old name Madeira describes a historical naming tradition and does not make this a Portuguese Madeira vinifera variety.

summary: An uncommon German red used for light reds and refreshing Weissherbst, better known as a parent of Dornfelder.
origin: Bred by August Herold at Weinsberg in 1929; registered in 1960, with breeding designation We S 130.
viticulture: Strong upright growth with few lateral shoots; large, fairly compact bunches and firm skins. Freytag rates it mid-ripening but early-colouring, with useful winter hardiness and downy-mildew tolerance.
winemaking: Made as light red wine or Weissherbst rosé; commercial examples include off-dry styles. Colour and residual sugar are wine-specific.
taste: Reds are generally light and gently fruity; rosé examples can emphasise refreshing acidity.

confusions: Crossed with Helfensteiner to produce Dornfelder; Heroldrebe is a specific variety, not a collective term for Herold’s cultivars.

summary: Violet, wild fruit, dried leaves and a slight smokiness form a distinctive profile. Known as Humagne Rouge in Switzerland and associated with the name Cornalin in Aosta.
origin: From the Aosta Valley, introduced to Valais in the late nineteenth century.
viticulture: Swiss plantings are almost entirely in Valais. Ripeness and yield require assessment by site; the viticultural characteristics of Humagne Blanche must not be transferred to this variety.
winemaking: Principally dry red wines. Ripeness and gentle extraction help combine its wild-fruit character with fine tannins.
taste: Violet, elderberry, dried vine leaves and smoke, with a juicy palate, tannins and some bitterness.
geneticsNote: One confirmed parent is Rouge du Pays / Cornalin du Valais; the other is unknown. A single-parent relationship must not be presented as a complete pedigree.
confusions: Not a direct colour mutation of Humagne Blanche, and not Petit Rouge. Cornalin du Valais is its known parent; Cornalin d’Aoste is this variety itself.

summary: An aromatic German white with high must-sugar potential and notable botrytised sweet-wine applications.
origin: Bred by Georg Scheu at Alzey in 1927; named for Fritz Huxel, who promoted plantings in the 1950s.
viticulture: Early-ripening, vigorous and potentially productive; large bunches vary in compactness with fruit set. Sensitive to winter frost, fungal disease and high lime; thin-skinned small berries can support noble rot.
winemaking: Used for aperitif and dessert wines; acidity can sustain freshness and ageing in noble-sweet examples. High sugar potential does not prescribe sweetness.
taste: Passion fruit, mango, peach and spice; assess acidity, sugar and concentration together in sweet examples.
geneticsNote: VIVC marker-supported parents are Elbling (Elbling Weiss) × Muscat Précoce de Saumur; Gutedel × Courtiller Musqué remains an older attribution in some publications.
confusions: Do not import historically misidentified parents as synonyms. Huxelrebe, Scheurebe and Faberrebe are separate Alzey cultivars.

summary: A minor Ostuni-area white traditionally blended with other local white grapes.
origin: Recorded around Ostuni, Carovigno, Cisternino and Ceglie Messapica; local history associates its arrival from Martina Franca with a grower nicknamed Impigno.
viticulture: Intermediate-early ripening; good vigour, preference for deep soils, thin-skinned obovoid berries.

summary: Known as Isabelle in French legal texts, this is a black-berried American hybrid with both wine and table uses. Historic; excluded from EU wine-grape classification under Article 81.
origin: An American grape introduced by William Prince after he encountered vines supplied by Isabella Gibbs around 1816. South Carolina is the traditional origin, but Hedrick records uncertainty over the precise discovery locality.
viticulture: New York observations describe late budburst, large black berries and later ripening than Concord. Vigour and yield varied, while mildew and black rot were concerns. Thick skins, persistent berries and good keeping quality supported table use.
winemaking: UC Davis lists wine and table use. Historical European wine production is documented, but the French connection is historical and conservation-related rather than a current authorization claim.
taste: The historical New York description notes musky, foxy fruit character, sweetness with tartness toward the berry centre, and astringency when underripe. These describe berries, not a universal finished-wine profile.
geneticsNote: Current VIVC lists labrusca × Meslier Petit. The VIVC EU name cross-reference equates Meslier Petit #7675 with French Petit Meslier. This is more specific than the older broad labrusca × vinifera description; an Ives attribution from later non-peer-reviewed work is not adopted here.
confusions: Isabelle is the legal French spelling of this entry. Uva Fragola and similar strawberry-grape names can be loose vernacular labels and should not identify an unknown vine without confirmation.

summary: A dark-skinned American hybrid historically planted in France for fruit and as a rootstock. Historic; excluded from EU wine-grape classification under Article 81.

viticulture: Hedrick’s Lenoir account describes vigorous vines suited to a long, warm season, with winter tenderness and some rot susceptibility limiting northern culture. Drought tolerance and phylloxera resistance were historically valued, without implying universal pest immunity.
winemaking: Historical accounts associate it with dark red wine. The US TTB petition record documents Jacquez and Black Spanish as names for Lenoir in Texas and other southern states; that nomenclature is not evidence of French authorization.
taste: The historical description emphasizes strong colour and subacidly sweet fruit. A detailed modern wine aroma profile is not supplied by the primary records used here.
geneticsNote: VIVC classifies Jacquez as an interspecific grape; historical botanical descriptions place it in the bourquiniana group with American and vinifera affinities. No pair of named cultivar parents is asserted.
confusions: Do not merge with Herbemont, despite historical confusion and overlapping old vernacular names. Jacquez à Gros Grains is also a separate named accession, not automatically a synonym.

summary: A shared parent of Merlot and Malbec, and a key discovery in research on Bordeaux varieties. Long overlooked, it now has value for germplasm conservation and understanding the inheritance of ripening time.
origin: An old western French grape, formerly surviving in scattered locations across the west.
viticulture: Relatively early-ripening, with moderate vigour. Long pruning gives better fruit set; spur pruning can produce low yields. Early ripening reduces grey-rot pressure, although bird damage warrants attention.
winemaking: Few modern vinification examples are publicly documented. Technical observations support coloured, structured reds; no representative commercial brands are invented.
taste: Official observations identify black fruit and liquorice, medium to relatively low acidity, and some fruit complexity. Further assessment across sites and vintages is needed.
geneticsNote: Its own parents are not confirmed here. It produced Merlot with Cabernet Franc and Malbec with Prunelard.
confusions: Do not merge it with other early-ripening table grapes called Madeleine. The spelling Magdeleine must be matched precisely to the germplasm identity.

summary: An Isère heritage red combining colour, tannin and moderate sugar potential.
origin: From Isère, also documented under the historical name Mècle de Bourgoin.
viticulture: Fairly vigorous and semi-upright, suitable for long pruning. Susceptible to grey rot. Vassal: budbreak +1 day; maturity +3 weeks versus Chasselas. Clone 1410 was approved in 2025.

taste: Well coloured, tannic and structured; no detailed primary-source aroma list is available.
geneticsNote: The consulted primary profile does not establish a complete parent pair.
confusions: Mescle is an official propagation synonym; Mècle de Bourgoin is historical usage, not a separate entry.

summary: The principal grape of Muscadet, usually aromatically restrained and focused on freshness and texture. Fine sites and long lees ageing can provide complexity and ageing capacity.
origin: Bourgogne–Franche-Comté, France; its modern heartland is around Nantes.
viticulture: Suited to relatively cool regions. Susceptible to grey rot; compact bunches and damp conditions require management. Pruning should account for basal-bud fertility.
winemaking: Usually made as dry white wine. Sur lie and longer lees ageing can increase texture, bready notes and ageing capacity.
taste: Citrus, green apple and subtle flowers; usually light to medium body and evident acidity. Lees-derived texture is often more prominent than intense aroma.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape records a natural crossing of Pinot and Gouais Blanc.
confusions: Muscadet is distinct from Muscat and Muscadelle. The name Melon does not mean that the wine must taste of melon.

summary: Capable of expressing floral aromas, fresh fruit and differences of site. Slope-grown wines from Bierzo and Ribeira Sacra offer useful comparisons with Jaen from Portugal’s Dão.

taste: Red cherry, raspberry, violet-like flowers and herbs. Body and tannin vary with yield and extraction.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage was not verified in the regional and producer sources reviewed for this entry. This does not imply that no scientific research exists.
confusions: Not Cabernet Franc. Historical speculation based on flavour similarity does not replace DNA identification.

summary: Combines ripe plum fruit with rounded texture, but does not inherently mean simplicity, low acidity or limited ageing capacity. Fine Right Bank Bordeaux sites can produce deeply structured Merlot.
origin: Bordeaux, France.
viticulture: Relatively early budding and ripening. Spring frost, coulure at flowering and rot near harvest require attention. Sugar can accumulate rapidly in warm vintages.

taste: Plum, black cherry and red berries; with maturity, chocolate, earth and tobacco may appear. Body, alcohol and tannin vary widely.
geneticsNote: Genetic analysis supports the stated parents.
confusions: Merlot blanc is not a white mutation of Merlot. Some historical Chilean “Merlot” plantings were actually Carmenère.

summary: A separate Bordeaux white grape, rather than white Merlot.
origin: Developed in the Bordeaux vineyard.
viticulture: Highly fertile and consistently productive but drought-sensitive. Very susceptible to grey rot; ungrafted sandy-soil vines can suffer root-knot nematodes. Vassal: budbreak +2 days, maturity +3 weeks versus Chasselas.
winemaking: A Bordeaux auxiliary white grape producing comparatively neutral wine; grey-rot sensitivity makes healthy fruit important.
taste: Relatively neutral; the primary profile reports modest quality potential rather than a distinctive aromatic signature.
confusions: A Folle Blanche–Merlot offspring, not a colour mutation of Merlot.
geneticsNote: Montpellier analyses indicate this cross; Plantgrape retains conditional wording.

summary: An Italian resistant selection registered in France under its UD breeding code.
origin: University of Udine–IGA breeding, developed with VCR; French classification in 2022.
viticulture: Medium budbreak and ripening in VCR trials. Strong vigour, semi-upright; fertile basal buds; canopy work is important. Strong downy-mildew resistance, good powdery resistance; botrytis, acid rot, black rot and Phomopsis remain concerns.
winemaking: High sugar, moderate acidity and substantial phenolics support ageing.
taste: Red fruit, deep ruby colour and full structure.
geneticsNote: Direct cross given by the breeder; the UD code and commercial name identify the same variety.
confusions: A distinct bred variety, not a clone of its familiar vinifera parent.

summary: Formerly more prominent in Veronese blends, and still used in some Bardolino and Valpolicella wines. Typically contributes freshness and relatively pale colour.
origin: A traditional variety from around Verona in Veneto, Italy.
viticulture: The skins often carry a conspicuous waxy bloom. Yield and fruit health require management appropriate to the site.
winemaking: Mostly used as a blending component. Varietal wines are uncommon; the full characteristics of the variety cannot be inferred from a single blend.
taste: Delicate red fruit, relatively light body and marked acidity are common impressions.

geneticsNote: A probable Gouais Blanc descendant in Plantgrape; the other parent is not established here.
confusions: Historical spellings include Molard; name similarity alone does not identify Iberian grapes called Mollar.

summary: A rare Alpine white variety of particular importance in the pedigrees of Syrah and Mondeuse Noire. Blanche does not mean that it is simply a colour mutation of Mondeuse Noire.
origin: Savoie, France.
viticulture: Drooping shoots and relatively late ripening, with comparatively low susceptibility to grey rot. Medium-sized bunches and berries; harvest timing must secure ripeness without losing balance.
winemaking: Small-scale still whites and conservation plantings. Good sugar accumulation can produce relatively high alcohol, while acidity is generally moderate.
taste: Some aromatic expression at maturity, but published variety descriptions do not establish a consistent, detailed list of signature aromas. Ripe fruit, moderate acidity and relatively high sugar potential are the main points.
geneticsNote: Its own complete parentage is unconfirmed. It is a parent of Syrah with Dureza, and of Mondeuse Noire with Tressot.
confusions: Mondeuse Blanche and Mondeuse Noire are distinct varieties and must not be merged as colour mutations.

summary: The grey-berried mutation of Mondeuse Noire, suitable for dry white and rosé wines.

taste: Quince and stone-fruit aromas are documented, with good freshness.
geneticsNote: A berry-colour mutation of Mondeuse Noire.
confusions: Mondeuse Blanche is a separate variety; it is not the white member of this mutation series.

summary: High acidity, pronounced tannins and spice give a distinctive mountain-red profile. Deep colour and strong structure do not necessarily require very high alcohol.
origin: Savoie, France.
viticulture: Relatively vigorous, suited to short pruning. Sensitive to drought and iron chlorosis; adapted to stony slopes and clay-limestone scree.

taste: Dark berries, violet, pepper and spice. Acidity and tannins are both pronounced, with moderate sugar potential.
geneticsNote: Current Pl@ntGrape information gives these parents on the basis of genetic analysis in Montpellier.
confusions: Mondeuse Blanche is not its white mutation: it is a distinct variety and one of its parents. Mondeuse is also distinct from Refosco.

summary: Often contributes floral aromas and softness in small proportions to Bordeaux whites. In Rutherglen, Australia, it produces concentrated fortified sweet wines with a very different expression.

summary: A traditional white of Wachau and Thermenregion, known for substance and nutty development.
origin: Probably originated in Austria’s Wachau; its local history is commemorated at Arnsdorf.
viticulture: Mid-season budburst, early-to-mid flowering and mid-season ripening. Short, compact bunches with green-yellow berries; good dry sites suit it, while deep fertile soils can encourage excess vigour and poor fruit set. Risks include winter frost, wind breakage, Botrytis and splitting; a decline syndrome involving shortened internodes is also documented.
winemaking: Produces substantial dry whites and Prädikat wines; style depends on ripeness and fruit health.
taste: Floral and spicy when young, with substantial body and increasingly nutty development.
geneticsNote: A natural Vitis vinifera crossing of Roter Veltliner × Silvaner.

summary: A pale-berried American hybrid important in the history of French direct producers. Historic; excluded from EU wine-grape classification under Article 81.
origin: Otto Wasserzieher raised Noah at Nauvoo, Illinois, from Taylor seed sown in 1869; first fruit was reported in 1873. It subsequently reached French vineyards as a direct producer and rootstock.
viticulture: The New York station recorded very late budburst and ripening with or after Concord, with productive vines but berry shatter and poor transport performance. Its observations also include mildew susceptibility and damage in severe winters: historical resistance claims should not become a blanket immunity claim.
winemaking: Historically used in France for wine and brandy, as well as for rootstocks. Its historical role is the subject here; it is not presented as a currently authorized French commercial wine grape.
taste: Hedrick describes the fresh fruit as juicy, tart and showing labrusca-like foxiness, less pronounced than in Elvira. These are historical berry observations, not a verified modern wine tasting profile.
geneticsNote: VIVC records Taylor open pollination. The pollen parent is unassigned here; historical descriptions indicate riparia and labrusca ancestry, not a proven Taylor × Hartford pedigree.
confusions: Do not merge with Taylor or Elvira. Similar pale berries conceal different vine and fruit characters.

taste: Coloured, balanced wines; no specific fruit signature is established in the technical profile.

summary: Produces both fresh, delicate dry whites and Vino Santo Trentino from grapes dried for an exceptionally long period. These two styles represent important aspects of the variety.
origin: A traditional local white grape of Trentino, Italy.
viticulture: Found principally in Valle dei Laghi and Pressano, often trained to pergola or Guyot. Local ventilation is important both for fruit health and for drying the harvested grapes.
winemaking: Used for dry white wine and for Vino Santo Trentino after prolonged grape drying. It is not a prescribed universal grape for Tuscan Vin Santo.
taste: Apple, delicate floral notes and hazelnut. Sweet versions develop dried apricot, honey and a concentrated texture.
geneticsNote: The complete parentage has not been verified for this entry; similar names and local traditions are not treated as evidence of genetic relationships.
confusions: Vino Santo Trentino and Tuscan Vin Santo are distinct regional traditions; their grapes and drying methods must be checked separately.

summary: A rare Lot white with late budburst and useful blending freshness.
origin: Probably from Lot; French catalogue entry in 2018.
viticulture: Productive and semi-upright; late budburst reduces spring-frost exposure. Little grey-rot sensitivity. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +15 days; maturity +4½–5 weeks.
winemaking: Compact medium-to-large clusters; berries cling to the pedicel. Best considered for fresh blending rather than long ageing.
taste: Low alcohol and lively freshness; it can lift a blend.

origin: An old Sardinian white grape, especially around Cagliari and Oristano. Phoenician introduction through Nora remains a hypothesis.
summary: An adaptable, potentially high-yielding island white grape, ranging from fresh steel-fermented wines to more textural lees- or barrel-influenced examples.
viticulture: Robust across several soil types and capable of abundant yields; site and crop level influence the finished style.
winemaking: Pala’s Milleluci uses steel fermentation and lees contact; Perlia illustrates large-barrel fermentation. These are producer choices, not mandatory varietal methods.
taste: Often white flowers, green apple and citrus, with moderate alcohol and freshness; barrel and lees work can alter texture.

summary: A rare aromatic white, notably preserved as a varietal wine by Zahel in Vienna and used as a parent of Goldburger.
origin: Selected around 1840 by Johann Philipp Bronner from wild vines between Rastatt and Speyer on the German Rhine. Zahel replanted a varietal vineyard in 1966.
viticulture: Preserved in Viennese mixed vineyards. Zahel’s Maurerberg example grows on flysch sandstone over dolomitic limestone; this is a site description, not a universal soil requirement.
winemaking: Used in varietal whites and mixed vineyards. Zahel’s 2025 uses brief skin contact and stainless-steel fine-lees ageing; the name does not imply prolonged skin-macerated orange wine.
taste: Typically aromatic and substantial, potentially low in acidity; producer descriptions include orange blossom and stone fruit. Vintage and harvest determine balance.
geneticsNote: Molecular markers support a natural Pinot × Chasselas crossing within Vitis vinifera; it is also a parent of Goldburger.
confusions: Orangetraube is a cultivar; orange wine is a production style. It is not a synonym of Goldburger.

summary: An early-ripening, sugar-accumulating German white represented by German sweet wines and English still whites.
origin: Bred at Bavaria’s wine and horticulture institute in 1948; Biddenden planted it in 1969 and has produced Ortega wine since 1972.
viticulture: Early ripening and capable of high must weights even in less favourable seasons; acidity falls quickly in warm years, requiring close harvest monitoring.
winemaking: Used for high-ripeness sweet wines in Germany; England also produces dry and off-dry still examples and sweet sparkling styles.
taste: Can show peach and other stone fruit; English examples add green apple, grapefruit and floral notes. Body and acidity vary with climate and picking.
geneticsNote: Müller-Thurgau × Siegerrebe, a deliberately bred crossing within Vitis vinifera.
confusions: Siegerrebe is a parent, not a synonym; early ripening does not guarantee low alcohol or a sweet style.

summary: A black-berried hybrid widely discussed as a direct producer in historical French viticulture. Historic; excluded from EU wine-grape classification under Article 81.
origin: The historical Othello account traces Charles Arnold’s breeding at Paris, Ontario, to seed sown in 1859. Modern VIVC identity records require care: Othello and Othello Arnold have separate accession identities.
viticulture: Hedrick’s historical material was vigorous and usually productive, with large bunches and late maturity. Fungal susceptibility varied with locality; late ripening limited its suitability in New York. These observations should be attached to the historical material, not assumed for every vine bearing the name.
winemaking: The 1908 account reports ordinary, well-coloured wine and former French use both as direct producer and, to a lesser degree, rootstock. Modern cultivar-wide processing prescriptions are not established by that account.
taste: Historical descriptions report foxy fruit flavour and strongly coloured wine. No modern producer-specific aroma or tannin profile is asserted.
geneticsNote: Hedrick reports Clinton × Black Hamburg for Arnold’s Othello. Current VIVC separates Othello #8838 from Othello Arnold #26119; the latter is listed with Clinton and Schiava Grossa. The parent array remains empty until the intended material is resolved.
confusions: Othello Arnold is a separate current VIVC record, not silently merged here. The historical name Black Hamburg also needs context; do not automatically substitute Muscat Hamburg.

taste: Deep ruby with cherry, forest fruit, plum and herbs; youthful wines can be markedly acidic and gripping.

summary: A rare Gironde-associated red with high cropping capacity.
origin: Possibly native to Gironde; entered the French catalogue in 2014.
viticulture: Vigorous, productive and upright to semi-upright, with little coulure. Overcropping impairs ripening. Sensitive to downy mildew, anthracnose and grey rot. Vassal: budbreak +6 days, maturity +3 weeks versus Chasselas.
winemaking: Red-wine use with modest alcohol potential; controlling crop load is central to ripeness.
taste: Often low in freshness; berries can have a slightly herbaceous flavour.
confusions: French classification and possible Gironde origin do not establish Bordeaux AOC authorization.

summary: A source of lightness and finesse in traditional Cava blends. Its contribution usually lies in freshness, perfume and delicacy rather than varietal weight.

winemaking: Primarily used in traditional-method sparkling blends; timely harvest preserves delicacy.
taste: Subtle flowers, white fruit and citrus; usually light and fresh.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage was not verified in the regional and producer sources reviewed for this entry. This does not imply that no scientific research exists.
confusions: Distinct from Macabeo and Xarel·lo. The traditional Cava trio should not be assumed to form a single genetic family.

origin: Western Piedmont around Saluzzo’s Val Bronda and Pagno, and Chieri near Turin; distinct from Verduno’s Pelaverga Piccolo.
summary: A large-berried local red grape, formerly used for the table, now giving pale red or rosé wines in dry and slightly sweet styles.
viticulture: Mid-late to late ripening. Moderate vigour; large bunches drive good productivity. Large berries; Guyot is usual, with small pergolas also traditional. Rain during ripening can favour grey mould and other bunch rots.
winemaking: May be vinified alone; extraction and residual-sugar decisions determine pale red, rosé, dry or slightly sweet expressions.
taste: Pale ruby-violet colour, distinctive perfume and generally moderate acidity; do not transfer Pelaverga Piccolo’s pepper description uncritically.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage has not been verified in the sources consulted for this record.
confusions: Genetically distinct from Pelaverga Piccolo. Peilavert in Canavese/Biella can denote Neretto Duro; Cari is the Chieri name.

summary: An important member of Champagne’s rare white varieties, contributing pronounced acidity and finesse. Its Gouais Blanc and Savagnin parentage makes it a useful reference in grape genealogy.
origin: Northern France.
viticulture: Early budding and vulnerable to spring frost. Coulure and millerandage may occur; very susceptible to grey rot. Better suited to long pruning and well-exposed, sunny sites.
winemaking: Small bunches and berries, with a relatively low juice yield. Used for dry whites and high-quality traditional-method sparkling base wines; varietal Champagnes also exist.
taste: Lively acidity. Comité Champagne describes citrus and smoky associations; lees contact, fermentation and maturation also influence the finished wine’s aromas.
geneticsNote: Plantgrape confirms Gouais Blanc × Savagnin Blanc from published genetic analyses. A natural cross, not a modern breeding creation.
confusions: Petit Meslier and Meslier Saint-François are different varieties; their shared Meslier name does not justify merging them.

summary: High acidity, a substantial palate and a saline finish can coexist. An important reference for the diversity of indigenous Swiss whites, with both dry and sweet expressions.
origin: Long associated with Valais, with documentation dating to the seventeenth century.
viticulture: Sensitive to spring frost and wind. Favours sunny, well-drained slopes; low-lying wet sites are less suitable.
winemaking: Dry wines, late-harvest wines and sweet wines from dried grapes. Sweetness must be assessed from the individual wine, not inferred from the grape name.
taste: Grapefruit, rhubarb, passion fruit and floral notes are common. Pronounced acidity can accompany an almost creamy, rounded palate and a saline impression on the finish.
geneticsNote: The sources reviewed for this entry do not establish both parents; no unverified parentage is supplied.
confusions: Petite Arvine must not be merged with other local material containing Arvine in its name solely on that basis. Salinity is a sensory description, not proof that a particular soil substance passes directly into the wine.

summary: A revived Savoyard white with floral and honeyed expression.

taste: Expressive floral and honeyed aromas.

summary: A scarce southern white, known in Châteauneuf-du-Pape blends.
origin: Native to southern France.
viticulture: Moderate vigour, semi-upright; short-prune, preferably trellis, on dry low-fertility warm sites. Magnesium deficiency and powdery mildew matter; some grey rot. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +5 days; maturity +3½–4 weeks.
winemaking: Large bunches and berries; low-to-moderate sugar potential supports a restrained blending contribution.
taste: Fruity, fairly fine and moderately acidic. Domaine Ampelhus describes quince, almond blossom and a slight musky note in its varietal bottling; these are wine-specific observations.
geneticsNote: The cited technical record does not establish a complete parentage.
confusions: Not Piquepoul Blanc; Araignan is the documented synonym here.

summary: A Beaujolais research cross with late budding and concentrated reds.
origin: INRA/SICAREX Beaujolais cross from the 1980s, listed in France in 2014.
viticulture: Vigorous, semi-upright and suitable for short pruning; many secondary bunches. Sensitive to both mildews, less to grey rot. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +16 days; maturity +2 weeks.

geneticsNote: Bred from Pinot Noir × Cabernet Sauvignon by INRA/SICAREX Beaujolais.

summary: Valued for its sparse bunches and low yields, and best known for sweet wine. Typical expressions combine complex floral and fruit notes, honey and a concentrated texture.
origin: A traditional white grape of Friuli, Italy.
viticulture: Problems with flower development and fruit set result in low yields and small, loose bunches. Careful selection is necessary at harvest.
winemaking: Usually made into sweet wine or sweet wine from dried grapes. Methods of concentration and ageing vary by producer.
taste: Apricot, dried fruit, honey and flowers; sweetness and concentration are usually prominent.
geneticsNote: The complete parentage has not been verified for this entry; similar names and local traditions are not treated as evidence of genetic relationships.
confusions: Picolit is not an alternative name for Glera, the principal grape of Prosecco. Sparse bunches should not automatically be attributed to noble rot.

summary: An Italian white grape suited to both sparkling and still wine. Grechetto Gentile, Grechetto di Todi and Rimini’s Rebola are local names for the same variety. Its fresh fruit character suits light, lively wines, while selected hillside fruit can produce structured still whites capable of ageing.
origin: A historic Italian variety, particularly associated with local vine material in the Bolognese hills and Todi in Umbria. Ancient wine names alone cannot establish its precise place of origin.
viticulture: Moderate vigour, mid-season budbreak and mid-to-late ripening. Bunches are relatively compact, with small oval berries and resilient skins. Suited to well-drained hillsides that are not excessively dry; sensitive to drought, with yields that can be inconsistent.
winemaking: Produces still, lightly sparkling and fully sparkling wines. Sparkling production may use tank or bottle secondary fermentation. Retaining acidity and delicate floral and fruit aromas is central to fresh styles; more structured still wines may benefit from longer maturation.
taste: Typically delicate apple, white flowers and fresh green notes, with clear acidity. Styles range from light sparkling wines to persistent, more structured still whites. Clone, ripeness and winemaking influence both acidity and aromatic intensity.
geneticsNote: Morphological and microsatellite evidence supports the identification of these local names as synonyms of the same variety. The complete parentage has not been verified for this entry; local synonyms should not be misrepresented as a crossing.
confusions: Distinct from Grechetto di Orvieto, Greco di Tufo, Pinot Blanc and Welschriesling/Riesling Italico. Pignoletto also appears in appellation and wine names; grape identity must be distinguished from the name on a label.

summary: Delicate floral aromas can accompany a full palate and pronounced acidity. Increasingly bottled as a varietal wine rather than used only in blends.

taste: Jasmine, peach, pineapple and grapefruit, with marked acidity and a potentially rounded, oily texture.

summary: Noted for delicate, restrained fruit and rounded texture, in both still whites and sparkling wines. Its expression depends more on acidity, texture and site than on pronounced varietal aromatics.
origin: A white-berried mutation of Pinot Noir.
viticulture: Adapted to relatively cool conditions. Yield control and healthy fruit are important; compact bunches make rot management a priority.
winemaking: Stainless steel can preserve fresh fruit, while lees contact and oak can add texture. Also used for traditional-method sparkling wines.
taste: Apple, pear, citrus and gentle floral notes. Usually medium in acidity and body; oak and lees can contribute bread and nut notes.
geneticsNote: A white-skin mutation, distinct from Chardonnay.
confusions: Under local rules, Alsace wines labelled Pinot Blanc may include Auxerrois. The label term should not be taken as a guarantee of varietal purity.

summary: The same variety can produce light, fresh wines or rich, full-bodied styles. Common differences between Alsace and Italian examples largely reflect site, yield, harvest timing and winemaking choices.
origin: A grey- or pink-skinned mutation within the Pinot family, historically associated with Burgundy.
viticulture: Relatively early ripening, with strong sugar accumulation. Skins range from grey-pink to deep copper; acidity at maturity is often lower than in Riesling.
winemaking: Direct pressing produces pale white wines; skin contact can produce copper-coloured ramato. Late-harvest and botrytised sweet wines are also made. The grape name does not determine sweetness.
taste: Pear, apple, peach and spice. Rich examples can show smoke and honey. Acidity and residual sugar vary considerably with style.
geneticsNote: A colour mutation of Pinot Noir, not a cross between Pinot Noir and another variety.
confusions: Pinot Grigio and Pinot Gris are the same variety. Ramato describes a copper-coloured skin-contact style, not a separate grape.
