summary: An important Champagne variety, often contributing fruit and softness. Single-variety, single-site wines can also express soil and develop complexity with age; its role is not limited to supporting blends.
origin: A mutation within the Pinot family distinguished by hairiness, traditionally associated with northern France.
viticulture: Relatively late budding and capable of early ripening, with good winter cold tolerance. Secondary buds retain some fruitfulness after spring frost. Leaf hairs are an identification feature.
winemaking: Common in traditional-method sparkling blends, with varietal Champagne and still red wines also produced. Lees ageing and oxidation management create different textures.
taste: Apple, pear, red fruit and flowers. Sparkling examples often offer accessible fruit. Ageing potential depends on site, ripeness and winemaking.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape describes it as a mutation of Pinot, chiefly distinguished by hairiness. It is not a Pinot × Riesling cross.
confusions: Schwarzriesling is not a black Riesling. Meunier’s ageing potential should not be judged solely by varietal stereotypes.

summary: Sensitive to site and vintage, producing refined still reds as well as traditional-method sparkling wines. Pale colour does not imply weak flavour or limited ageing potential.
origin: Traditionally associated with an origin in Burgundy, France; a member of the ancient Pinot family.
viticulture: Early budding and early ripening. Small, compact bunches and thin skins bring frost and rot risks. Clone, yield and canopy management have substantial effects.
winemaking: Destemming versus whole-bunch fermentation, maceration intensity and oak selection can markedly alter style. Direct pressing is common for sparkling base wines.
taste: Cherry, strawberry and flowers, developing woodland, mushroom and leather with maturity. Acidity is often pronounced, with fine rather than heavy tannins.
geneticsNote: Unverified hypotheses about ancient origins are not presented as established parents. Pinot Gris, Pinot Blanc and Meunier are related mutations.
confusions: Pinot colour mutations must be distinguished from independent crosses. Pinot Noir and Pinotage are not the same variety.

summary: A coloured-flesh form within Pinot, explaining the name in Romorantin parentage records. It does not represent all teinturier grapes or all conventional Pinot Noir clones.
origin: A coloured-flesh mutation within the Pinot family; included here to clarify pedigrees.
viticulture: Published research confirms very close genetic similarity to Pinot. This entry does not have sufficient primary evidence to establish independent, generally applicable ripening or disease-resistance parameters.
winemaking: Coloured flesh is the key identifying characteristic. No independent commercial wine style, representative estate or fixed vinification protocol is invented here.
taste: Insufficient independent varietal-wine evidence across vintages to support a fixed flavour profile. The focus is the flesh-colour mutation and genetic identity.
geneticsNote: UC Davis FPS describes Pinot Fin Teinturier as a Pinot form with coloured juice. Its SSR profile is essentially the same as Pinot, with only isolated allelic differences.
confusions: Teinturier is a general description of coloured flesh, whereas Pinot Teinturier identifies a particular Pinot form. It must not be merged with Teinturier du Cher or Alicante Bouschet.

summary: A signature South African red variety, created by crossing Pinot Noir and Cinsaut. Styles range from fresh reds and rosé to concentrated, ageworthy wines and Cape Blends.
origin: Bred by Abraham Izak Perold in Stellenbosch, South Africa.
viticulture: Relatively early ripening. Yield, canopy management and harvest ripeness affect the balance of fruit, tannin and alcohol.
winemaking: Gentle extraction can produce fresh styles; barrel maturation is also common. “Coffee” expressions relate to winemaking and oak handling, rather than an intrinsic flavour present in every wine.
taste: Red berries, plum, black cherry and spice. Ripe, full styles and lighter, fresher expressions are both possible.
geneticsNote: Pinot Noir × Cinsaut. The Pinotage Association currently distinguishes the cross made in 1924 from the sowing of its seeds in 1925; 1925 remains the conventional date given for the variety’s birth.
confusions: The ending “-tage” derives from Hermitage, an old South African name for Cinsaut, not Rhône Syrah. Pinotage is not a Pinot Noir clone.

summary: A red whose modern DNA pedigree contradicts the historical Pinot-parent claim.
origin: Valentin Blattner breeding, subsequently selected and evaluated in Germany.
viticulture: Sources disagree on earliness: CIVARE calls it early, while nursery observations report later budbreak. Low–moderate vigour; loose elongated bunches. Carries Rpv3.1, Ren3 and Ren9; use regional observations to plan protection.
winemaking: Separate harvest decisions from Pinot Noir assumptions.
taste: Nursery observations describe ruby colour, dark cherry and a mild palate.
geneticsNote: Röckel et al. (2021) confirm Cabernet Sauvignon × Regent; the older CIVARE Pinot Noir × unknown account is obsolete.
confusions: The name is not proof of Pinot Noir parentage or sensory equivalence.

summary: Retains pronounced acidity in a warm Mediterranean environment and is the principal grape of Picpoul de Pinet. Usually encountered as a fresh, direct dry white.
origin: A white-berried mutation of the Piquepoul family of southern France.

taste: Lemon, green apple and subtle floral notes. Fresh acidity and light to medium body are common features.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape identifies it as a white-berried mutation of Piquepoul Noir.
confusions: Picpoul de Pinet is an appellation. Piquepoul Noir, Gris and Blanc should have separate variety records.

summary: A Dalmatian red grape associated with sunny, steep coastal slopes and pronounced ripeness. It is an offspring of Zinfandel, not the same variety.
origin: Dalmatia, Croatia.
viticulture: Late ripening and requires warmth. Sunburn, berry shrivelling and uneven ripening complicate the balance of sugar, acidity and tannins.
winemaking: Used for structured dry reds. Gentle extraction and oak maturation can help integrate the tannins.
taste: Blackberry, plum, fig and Mediterranean herbs, often with high alcohol and pronounced tannins.
geneticsNote: DNA research established Zinfandel, also known as Tribidrag, × Dobričić. This relationship does not make Plavac Mali identical to Zinfandel.
confusions: Do not merge it with Zinfandel. The shortened name Plavac may also have other local referents.

summary: A very early French cross for fruity, accessible young reds.

winemaking: Designed for early-drinking or primeur reds, with medium berries and clusters.
taste: Fruity, well-coloured, moderate in alcohol and low in tannin.
geneticsNote: INRA bred this cross in 1958: Garnacha Tinta × Portugais Bleu.

summary: Produces very pale reds with delicate aromas. Its light structure suits Jura cuisine, demonstrating that pale colour need not imply a lack of flavour.
origin: Jura, France.
viticulture: Relatively fragile, vulnerable to spring frost, coulure and high temperatures. Sensitive to powdery mildew. Suited to marl and limestone sites; requires support.
winemaking: Gentle maceration and careful oak use preserve delicate fruit. Made as a varietal wine, in local blends and in traditional sweet wines.
taste: Redcurrant, strawberry, flowers and light spice. Usually light-bodied and pale, with fine tannins; maturity can bring an onion-skin hue.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape notes a close relationship with Rèze. Neither a complete parentage nor the direction of the relationship is established in this entry.
confusions: Ploussard is a synonym. Trousseau is a distinct variety and often produces fuller-bodied wines.

summary: An early-ripening Alpine red capable of coloured, tannic wines for ageing.
origin: Native to Alpine vineyards; French catalogue registration dates to 2015.
viticulture: Vigorous, productive and semi-upright to upright; sometimes millerandes. Very sensitive to downy mildew, less to powdery mildew. Vassal: budbreak +5 days, maturity +1½–2 weeks versus Chasselas.
winemaking: Good sugar potential, limited acidity and firm tannin can support maturation; harvest decisions must consider acid retention.
taste: Coloured and tannic; the primary profile supports structure and ageing potential, not a specific aroma catalogue.
geneticsNote: Suggested Mondeuse Blanche × Tressot natural cross; conditional wording follows Plantgrape.
confusions: Salagnin is its official propagation synonym; this must not be conflated with Servagnin de Morges.

summary: An important Kefalonia dry-white variety, noted for fine acidity, restrained aromas and expression of origin. Its similar name does not make it the Italian Ribolla Gialla.
origin: A representative white variety of the Ionian Islands and Kefalonia, Greece.
viticulture: Susceptible to pests, diseases and drought, with relatively high yield potential. Poor hillside soils and yield control can support quality.
winemaking: Prone to oxidation; protective handling and stainless-steel vinification are commonly used to preserve freshness and a fine structure.
taste: Citrus, fresh fruit and mineral associations, with medium body. Specific flavours vary with ripeness and wine age.
geneticsNote: The sources reviewed for this entry do not establish both parents; no unverified parentage is supplied.
confusions: Robola and Ribolla Gialla must not be merged because of their similar names. Stories about geographical origins are not treated here as established parentage.

summary: A pink-skinned grape used for white wine. High-yielding lowland examples can differ substantially from wines grown in mountain sites with controlled yields.
origin: A pink-skinned variety widely grown in Greece.
viticulture: Crop control, altitude and harvest timing help avoid dilute flavours and insufficient freshness.
winemaking: Used for varietal dry whites, blends and traditional styles. A short period on the lees can add texture.
taste: Lemon, fruit peel and subtle stony impressions, with light to medium body. Good examples have crisp acidity.
geneticsNote: The complete parentage has not been verified in this edition; hypotheses are not presented as established findings.
confusions: Roditis is not Moschofilero. Skin colour alone does not determine the colour of the finished wine.

summary: The signature variety of Cour-Cheverny, noted for acidity, texture and ageing potential. Production is small, but its genealogy and geography are important.
origin: Historically associated with central France, with modern plantings concentrated in the Loire.
viticulture: Early budding, ripening slightly later than Chardonnay. Requires warm sites that allow reliable ripening, with controlled yields.
winemaking: Mainly dry whites, with late-harvest sweet examples possible. Lees contact and oak can add texture; ripeness affects the sharpness of the acidity.
taste: Citrus, apple and quince, developing beeswax, honey and nuts with age. Pronounced acidity and firm texture.
geneticsNote: Current Pl@ntGrape information specifies Pinot Teinturier × Gouais Blanc, rather than the broader term Pinot.
confusions: Cheverny and Cour-Cheverny have different white-wine rules and should not be conflated.

summary: A revived Corsican white, registered in France in 2020, with body and alcohol potential.
origin: Probably originates in southern Corsica.
viticulture: Vigorous, fertile, semi-erect to erect; some wind and drought sensitivity. Esca is a concern; limited mildew and grey-rot susceptibility is reported. Budbreak five days and maturity four to four and a half weeks after Chasselas at Vassal.
winemaking: Can build body in white blends; acidity may be insufficient.
taste: Full-bodied and persistent, with elevated alcohol potential and restrained aroma.
geneticsNote: The cited primary profile does not establish a complete pedigree.
confusions: Do not assume all historical Rossola names mean this cultivar; Ugni Blanc has also carried Corsican Rossola names.

summary: An old, pink-skinned white-wine speciality of Wagram, capable of substantial body and spice when yields are controlled.
origin: An old variety long associated with Austria; its precise geographical origin remains unresolved. Roman-origin accounts are not established fact.
viticulture: Mid-season budburst and flowering; late ripening. Pink-red skins with uncoloured flesh; vigorous, compact-bunched and potentially heavy or irregular yielding. Crop control is important; deep loess and good sites suit it. Sensitive at flowering, weak in winter frost; compact bunches increase Botrytis pressure.
winemaking: Used for white wine. Excessive crops dilute concentration; ripe, restricted yields can produce extract-rich, substantial wines.
taste: Spicy when young, developing almond notes with age. Riper examples are substantial; red skin does not imply red-wine character.
geneticsNote: Its parents are unresolved; it is a parent of Rotgipfler, Zierfandler, Neuburger and Frühroter Veltliner.
confusions: Not a colour mutation of Grüner Veltliner. Frühroter Veltliner is an offspring, not a synonym.

summary: A traditional Thermenregion white retaining acidity at substantial ripeness, made alone or blended with Zierfandler.
origin: Probably originated in Austria’s Thermenregion; historically associated with the white wines of Gumpoldskirchen.
viticulture: Mid-season budburst; mid-to-late flowering and ripening. Very compact bunches with oval, green-yellow berries; requires good sites and soils. Weak winter hardiness; particularly susceptible to downy mildew, with powdery mildew, Botrytis and splitting risks.
winemaking: Produces concentrated dry and Prädikat wines; traditionally blended with Zierfandler. Ripeness, potential alcohol and acidity must be considered together.
taste: Full-bodied and extract-rich, retaining acidity at ripeness; stronger examples develop in bottle.
geneticsNote: Traminer × Roter Veltliner, a natural crossing within Vitis vinifera.
confusions: Zierfandler is a separate variety and traditional blending partner, not a synonym.

origin: A white variety from Yonne.

winemaking: Still white wine; small bunches and berries.

taste: Pear, apricot, flowers, honey and herbal tea. Relatively full-bodied while retaining acidity, with nutty complexity developing through maturation.

summary: A pink-berried Provençal grape used in rosé blends; historically called Rosé du Var.
origin: Originates in Provence.

winemaking: Can yield white or lightly tinted low-alcohol wines and enter rosé blends. The CIVP lists it as a Côtes de Provence accessory.

summary: A rare Haute-Savoie white historically suited to sparkling-wine bases.
origin: Originates in Haute-Savoie; the name identifies the Ayze tradition rather than the Altesse grape.
viticulture: Fairly fertile under short pruning and adapted to glacial moraine soils. Sensitive to downy mildew and grey rot. Vassal: budbreak +5 days; maturity +1½ weeks versus Chasselas.
winemaking: Documented chiefly as material for sparkling base wines; its restrained aromatics can leave room for blend and lees-ageing effects.
taste: Relatively neutral and not strongly aromatic; the primary profile does not support an elaborate varietal aroma list.

confusions: Not Altesse, despite the shared word Roussette; also distinct from Gringet.

summary: An early-ripening Aveyron white with useful acidity.
origin: Native to Aveyron.

summary: Central Italy’s principal red grape, combining marked acidity, tannin and red-fruit aromas. Chianti, Brunello and Vino Nobile demonstrate different regional expressions.
origin: Italy, with clear historical records in Tuscany. Genetic research indicates close connections with a network of southern Italian varieties.
viticulture: Vigorous, requiring crop and canopy management. A warm, relatively dry ripening period favours fruit maturation; grey rot requires attention in damp conditions.
winemaking: Made as a varietal wine or blended with local varieties. Large casks, small barrels and the degree of maceration can substantially change texture and aroma.
taste: Cherry, violet, dried herbs and tea-like notes. Usually marked acidity and medium to high tannins, strongly influenced by ripeness and extraction.
geneticsNote: A 2021 SNP-based study rejected the earlier Ciliegiolo × Calabrese di Montenuovo parentage proposal. It identified Strinto porcino as a possible parent, but the complete parentage remains unresolved.
confusions: Brunello, Morellino and Prugnolo Gentile are not three distinct grape varieties. Sangiovese Grosso/Piccolo are traditional morphological groupings and cannot replace identification by clone and DNA.

summary: A productive aromatic hybrid requiring crop control and careful site interpretation.
origin: Valentin Blattner breeding from Switzerland; French catalogue entry in 2020.
viticulture: Vassal: budbreak +7 days; ripening +1 week versus Chasselas; German profiles describe later timing. Moderate vigour, productive; fragile shoots; magnesium/potassium deficiency; avoid overcropping. Generally low fungal susceptibility; bunch powdery mildew and sulfur-sensitive foliage need attention.
winemaking: White-wine styles vary with site and maturity; French wines may lack acidity.
taste: Citrus and tropical fruit; German reports also mention apple and apricot.
geneticsNote: A Sauvignon × Riesling descendant crossed with an unidentified hybrid; these are ancestors, not a confirmed three-parent direct cross.
confusions: Not Sauvignon Blanc; acidity differs between French and German observations.

summary: Noted for pronounced acidity and recognisable herbal, citrus or tropical-fruit aromas. Sancerre, Marlborough and barrel-aged Bordeaux whites provide useful comparisons.
origin: An ancient French variety, with traditional centres in the Loire and Bordeaux. Its precise birthplace is uncertain.
viticulture: Vigorous, requiring canopy and yield management. Compact bunches require grey-rot control. Shade and ripening conditions affect the balance between herbal and fruit aromas.
winemaking: Cool fermentation can emphasise fresh aromas. Barrel fermentation, lees ageing and blending with Sémillon are also used. Different techniques do not create a different grape variety.
taste: Lime, grapefruit, gooseberry and grass, with passion fruit in some regions. Usually high in acidity, with light to moderately full body.
geneticsNote: UC Davis FPS cites DNA research identifying Savagnin Blanc as one parent. The other parent is not established in this entry, so a complete cross is not presented.
confusions: Fumé Blanc does not guarantee oak use. Sauvignon and Savagnin are distinct varieties despite their similar spellings.

summary: Similar to Sauvignon Blanc, but often places greater emphasis on ripe fruit, body and texture. Made as a varietal wine or used to add weight to Bordeaux white blends.

summary: A signature white variety of Jura, but not inherently oxidative in flavour. Topped-up ouillé wines and sous-voile wines matured under a yeast film can have very different expressions.
origin: Possibly from Franche-Comté or the Pfalz in Germany; its precise origin remains uncertain.
viticulture: Small bunches and berries, with good sugar accumulation and acid retention. Requires full ripening; yields are usually modest.
winemaking: Can produce fresh or full-bodied dry whites. Vin Jaune requires a specific appellation context and extended maturation under a yeast film. Also used in some sweet wines.
taste: Topped-up examples can show citrus, apple and spice. Sous-voile versions often show walnut, curry and savoury notes, chiefly derived from maturation.
geneticsNote: A member of the ancient Traminer family. Unknown parents are not presented as established in this entry. Gewürztraminer represents an aromatic and colour mutation.
confusions: Savagnin is distinct from Sauvignon. Usage of Traminer across countries does not always distinguish aromatic from non-aromatic forms.

summary: Close to Gewürztraminer in appearance and genetic background, but without its pronounced rose, lychee and spicy aromatics. A separate record prevents all pink-skinned Traminer forms from being merged.
origin: A pink-skinned, non-aromatic mutation within the Savagnin family, now closely associated with Heiligenstein in Alsace.
viticulture: Similar to Gewürztraminer in habit. Suited to clay-limestone soils, although severe iron chlorosis must be avoided. Early-ripening, with small bunches and berries.
winemaking: Principally still white wines. Moderate lees maturation can add texture; Rose in its name does not automatically classify the wine as rosé.
taste: Relatively restrained aromatics, with an emphasis on texture and fine fruit. The official description explicitly notes the absence of Gewürztraminer’s characteristic spicy aromatics.
geneticsNote: Plantgrape explicitly identifies it as a pink-skinned, non-aromatic mutation of Savagnin Blanc.
confusions: Savagnin Rose and Gewürztraminer should be distinguished. Klevener de Heiligenstein must not automatically be merged with Klevner, a shortened name often referring to Pinot Blanc.

summary: An intensely aromatic white variety used for dry, late-harvest and noble-rot wines. Balance between aroma and acidity is central to its expression.
origin: Bred by Georg Scheu in 1916.
viticulture: Needs full ripeness; underripe fruit can be excessively herbal and acidic. Noble-rot styles require appropriate fruit health and botrytis development.
winemaking: Cool fermentation preserves aroma. Sweet wines gain concentration through late harvesting or noble rot.
taste: Blackcurrant, grapefruit, tropical fruit and flowers, with clearly defined acidity.
geneticsNote: Riesling × Bukettrebe. Before the clarification published in 2012, Silvaner was frequently and incorrectly identified as the other parent.
confusions: Sämling 88 is the same variety. The old Silvaner attribution should not be retained as established parentage.

origin: Long established in Corsica. Plantgrape equates it with Tuscan Mammolo, but a 2021 SNP study distinguishes the registered Mammolo clone I-MAM-PA-1.
viticulture: Moderate vigor; warm, relatively dry sites and controlled yields favor red-wine quality. Overripe berries shrivel rapidly. Budbreak six days and maturity three weeks after Chasselas at Vassal.
winemaking: Useful for red blends and rosé; good sugar accumulation can coexist with retained acidity.
taste: Relatively pale, fine and balanced; strawberry followed by spice is reported.
geneticsNote: Plantgrape reports this proposed pedigree from Italian genetic analysis. Accession identity must be checked before transferring Mammolo pedigrees.
confusions: Mammolo is an official synonym, but named accessions are not universally identical: the 2021 study found a parent–offspring relationship for I-MAM-PA-1 and Termarina/Sciaccarello.

viticulture: Moderate vigour and fertility, relatively loose bunches; trunk diseases warrant attention.
winemaking: Used for white wine and included among permitted grapes for Lourinhã wine spirit.

summary: A French cross for deeply coloured, robust reds, better suited to temperate conditions.
origin: INRA cross made in 1957.
viticulture: Weak vigour in southern conditions; better in temperate sites, trellised with moderately long pruning. Stem desiccation and magnesium deficiency, especially on SO4, need attention. Little grey rot. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +5 days; maturity +2 weeks.
winemaking: Medium bunches with very small berries provide strong extraction potential.
taste: Very deep colour, robust structure and marked tannin.
geneticsNote: INRA bred this cross in 1957: Jurançon Noir × Portugais Bleu.
confusions: Not a regional synonym of Jurançon Noir; it is a named deliberate cross.

summary: A historic French-classified variety with surviving cultivation documented by Plantgrape.

summary: A principal grape of Sauternes noble-rot sweet wines, also capable of producing very long-lived dry whites. Low-alcohol Hunter Valley examples, lean in youth, demonstrate the limits of fixed varietal style assumptions.
origin: Bordeaux, France.
viticulture: High yield potential. Thin skins favour useful noble rot in suitable conditions but also bring grey-rot risk. Temperature, humidity and harvest timing are critical.

taste: Lemon, wax and yellow fruit, developing toast and nuts with age. Botrytised examples can show honey, dried apricot and saffron.
geneticsNote: The official sources used for this entry do not provide both parents.
confusions: Toast in mature Hunter Sémillon does not necessarily indicate oak ageing. Muscadelle and Sémillon are not synonyms.

summary: Early ripening and strong sugar accumulation make it an important option for northern European viticulture. A disease-resistant breeding variety with interspecific ancestry, not a clone of a traditional variety.

summary: A modern disease-resistant variety with pink skins, usually made into white wine. Its DNA-based parentage correction is an important example of the revision of long-used pedigree descriptions.

summary: Offers a broad spectrum from pepper, violet and olive to ripe dark fruit. Syrah and Shiraz are the same variety; the name alone does not guarantee a particular body or style.

geneticsNote: DNA research supports these French parents, not the legend of an origin in Shiraz, Persia.
confusions: Petite Sirah usually refers to Durif, not a small-berried Syrah. Shiraz is not a separate grape.

summary: Known for abundant tannins and deeply coloured wines, with Madiran and Uruguay as two key references. Modern viticulture and extraction can preserve structure while making wines more approachable.
origin: Vineyards in the French Pyrenean foothills.
viticulture: Relatively vigorous, requiring support and balanced yields. Small to medium berries and relatively large bunches. Grey rot and mites require attention.
winemaking: Made as a varietal wine or blended with Cabernet varieties. Extraction, barrel ageing and micro-oxygenation may be used to manage tannins, but methods vary between wines.
taste: Blackberry, black plum and spice. Usually deeply coloured, with high tannins and pronounced acidity; fine examples can mature for many years.
geneticsNote: The official sources used for this entry do not establish both parents.
confusions: High tannins need not mean rough texture. Uruguayan and French examples should not be reduced to a fixed contrast between soft and hard styles.

summary: A rediscovered Gascon red with conspicuous peppery spice.
origin: Probably from Gascogne in Southwest France; entered the French catalogue in 2017.
viticulture: Moderately productive, semi-upright and best long-pruned; little grey-rot sensitivity. Vassal: budbreak with Chasselas, maturity +2½–3 weeks.
winemaking: IFV identifies it with the Saint-Mont heritage revival; small thick-skinned berries give structured red wine.
taste: Deep colour, strong pepper/spice, warmth and pronounced, sometimes astringent tannins.
confusions: The name means late, but phenology must be tied to the observation site rather than treated as a universal calendar.
geneticsNote: The cited profile does not establish complete parentage.

summary: Its name means “tongue-cutter”, referring to the acidity and tannin of young wines. One of Friuli’s local red varieties rescued from decline and brought back into use.
origin: A traditional local variety of Friuli, Italy.
viticulture: Grown mainly around Buttrio, Manzano, Rosazzo and Cividale. Ripeness and yield require careful balancing.
winemaking: Suited to dry red wine and ageing, which allows its firm texture to integrate.
taste: Dark-fruit flavours, with pronounced acidity and astringency when young; softer with age.
geneticsNote: The complete parentage has not been verified for this entry; similar names and local traditions are not treated as evidence of genetic relationships.
confusions: Not a synonym of Schioppettino or Pignolo.

summary: A central variety in Spanish red wine. Early ripening and stylistically versatile, it produces both fruit-driven young wines and structured reds capable of extended ageing.
origin: Spain; a principal red variety of Rioja and the Duero river basin.
viticulture: The name refers to early ripening. Thick-skinned; excessive heat, drought and disease can affect performance, so heat tolerance should not be treated as an absolute advantage.
winemaking: Vinified alone or blended with Garnacha, Graciano and Mazuelo. Oak maturation and bottle ageing often shape classic Rioja styles.
taste: Plum, strawberry, red and dark berries, with medium to high tannin. Vanilla, coconut and tobacco should be distinguished as oak-derived or age-related characteristics.
geneticsNote: ICVV and IMIDRA research confirmed Albillo Mayor × Benedicto through DNA markers. A naturally formed variety, rather than a product of modern deliberate breeding.
confusions: Distinct from Tempranillo Blanco, a separately maintained white mutation.

summary: A rare Provençal red retained as a Palette accessory.
origin: Originates in Provence.
viticulture: Erect and suited to gobelet and short pruning. Early budbreak creates spring-frost exposure; powdery mildew is a concern. Budbreak three days and maturity three weeks after Chasselas at Vassal.
winemaking: Large bunches and berries; authorized for Palette red and rosé blends.
taste: Deep color, moderate alcohol and relatively low acidity; refined aromatic detail is not established.
geneticsNote: Montpellier genetic analysis proposes Pougayen × Plant d’Entrechaux.
confusions: A rare local cultivar, not an alternate name for Tibouren.

summary: Deep purple colour and lively acidity make Teran distinctive in Istria. Modern examples can also be light and fine-textured; they should not all be characterized as rustic, heavy wines.
origin: Closely associated with historical cultivation and local red-wine traditions in Istria.
viticulture: Yield, site and ripeness affect concentration. The Kozlović example comes from limestone, clay and flysch sites in Istria.
winemaking: Can be vinified in stainless steel, with other maturation approaches also used. Gentle extraction can produce more approachable dry reds.
taste: Sour cherry, black cherry and woodland fruit, with lively acidity and tannins ranging from fine and supple to firm.
geneticsNote: The sources reviewed for this entry do not establish both parents; no unverified parentage is supplied.
confusions: Refosco has multiple meanings and must not automatically be equated with Teran; Refosco dal Peduncolo Rosso especially requires separate identification. Teran is also used as a geographical wine name in Slovenia, so label context matters.

summary: A deeply coloured, lively red variety important to Trentino. Concentration, acidity and aromatic expression often coexist.
origin: Northeastern Italy; now best known in Trentino’s Piana Rotaliana.
viticulture: Low fertility of the basal buds often requires long pruning. Favours well-drained sites with good ventilation; grey rot and sour rot require attention in wet years.
winemaking: Made in youthful, fruity styles or with longer ageing. Vessel choice and maceration intensity influence tannin texture.
taste: Blackberry, purple-fruit notes, light almond and spice, usually with deep colour and lively acidity.
geneticsNote: The complete parentage has not been verified for this entry; similar names and local traditions are not treated as evidence of genetic relationships.
confusions: Genetic relationships with Lagrein and Marzemino do not make them the same variety. This entry does not draw a conclusion on Teroldego’s complete parentage.

summary: A rare Madeira variety valued for fine, complex mature wines with tension. It has a distinct identity and style and should not be subsumed under a general Malvasia name.
origin: A traditional Portuguese white grape. Madeira’s Terrantez corresponds to Folgasão on the mainland.
viticulture: Thin skins and compact bunches make it susceptible to rot and berry splitting. Low yields and demanding cultivation.
winemaking: In Madeira, commonly made in medium-dry to medium-sweet styles. Extended oxidative maturation develops complexity.
taste: Fruit peel, spice, nuts and a complex bittersweet character, with freshness providing structural support.
geneticsNote: Complete parentage was not verified in the regional and producer sources reviewed for this entry. This does not imply that no scientific research exists.
confusions: Terrantez do Pico is a distinct Azorean variety name and should not be merged automatically.

summary: A rare Azorean white associated with Pico, revived through recent recovery and varietal bottling.
origin: A traditional Pico grape, not interchangeable with Terrantez names used in Madeira or mainland Portugal.
viticulture: IVV records early ripening, low vigour and small compact bunches; local growers particularly stress rot sensitivity and low yields.
winemaking: Can be vinified alone; potential alcohol and finished style depend on site and harvest, not one universal value.
taste: A local producer describes fresh, saline wines; actual acidity should be checked against the individual wine.
geneticsNote: The 2018 primary molecular study supports Verdelho × Bastardo; Bastardo is Trousseau.
confusions: Distinct from Terrantez da Terceira, a synonym of Arinto dos Açores, and Madeira’s Terrantez.

summary: Historically an important local white grape in Languedoc, now a source of freshness and restraint in blends. Its value often lies in acidity and balance rather than intense aromas.
origin: A white-berried mutation of the Terret family of southern France.
viticulture: Adapted to warm southern conditions. High yield potential requires site-specific control of vigour and crop levels. Ripeness and harvest timing affect style.
winemaking: Usually made as a dry white or used in southern French blends. The variety name alone does not indicate oak treatment or sweetness.
taste: Subtle citrus, green apple and herbs. Aromas are usually restrained, with a contribution of freshness.
geneticsNote: Pl@ntGrape identifies it as a white-berried mutation of Terret Noir.
confusions: Terret Blanc, Terret Gris and Terret Noir are related colour forms. A Terret label should not automatically be assigned to the same colour variety.

summary: The grey Terret mutation, preserved in Hérault and capable of low-alcohol wine.
origin: Grey mutation of Terret Noir.
viticulture: Similar to Terret Noir, with added browning susceptibility. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +9 days; maturity +4½–5 weeks. Large clusters and berries.
winemaking: Low alcohol potential and a neutral profile; distinguish berry colour from the finished wine category.
taste: Neutral, low-alcohol wines.
geneticsNote: A grey berry-colour mutation of Terret Noir.
confusions: Terret-Bourret belongs here; do not merge Terret Blanc and Gris.

origin: Native to Languedoc.
viticulture: Upright and suitable for gobelet or cordon. Susceptible to downy mildew, powdery mildew and wood diseases. At Vassal, relative to Chasselas: budburst +9 days; maturity +4½ weeks.
winemaking: Large clusters and medium berries; modest alcohol and colour suit lighter blends.
taste: Light-bodied, pale and low in alcohol.

summary: A Provençal specialty associated particularly with expressive, textured rosé.
origin: Traditionally grown in Provence; Plantgrape recognizes Rossese as its official Italian name.

winemaking: Usually rosé; also authorized as a Palette red and rosé accessory. Oxidative development can be part of the resulting style.
taste: Fruit and flowers, rounded body and persistence; oxidative notes may appear.
geneticsNote: The cited primary profile does not establish a complete pedigree.
confusions: Rossese is the documented Italian synonym; do not extend it to every white or red grape bearing a Rossese name.

summary: Contributes colour, ripe fruit and alcohol potential to Douro and Port blends. Often provides a softer tannin impression than some thicker-skinned blending partners.

summary: Roussillon’s Tourbat, called Torbato in Sardinia, combines body and acidity.

taste: Full-bodied and gently aromatic with retained freshness.
geneticsNote: The cited technical record does not establish a complete parentage.

origin: A traditional western Georgian white concentrated in central and upper Imereti and extensively described in historical ampelography.

summary: Often recognised by vivid fruit, fennel and a subtle bitter note. Styles include young dry whites, lees-aged and barrel-aged wines, and traditional oxidative expressions.

summary: A white variety bred for resistance to fungal diseases, carrying multiple genes associated with resistance to downy and powdery mildew. In Champagne it is a VIFA adaptation-trial variety, subject to planting, blending and monitoring conditions; this status differs from that of the traditional principal authorized varieties.
origin: An artificial interspecific cross from France’s INRA ResDur1 breeding programme, entered in the French variety catalogue in 2018.
viticulture: Vigorous, with moderate fertility, and suited to long pruning. Monitor magnesium and potassium deficiency and breakage at shoot nodes. Resistant to downy and powdery mildew but susceptible to black rot. Resistance does not remove the need for management; the breeder still recommends protective treatments to preserve resistance.
winemaking: Comité Champagne’s technical guidance requires blending in Champagne, with no more than 10% in the finished commercial wine. Plantings are generally limited to 5%, with calculation exemptions for specified plots adjoining sensitive areas. The variety name must not appear on the label, and vineyard and cellar technical monitoring is required.
taste: Berries have a relatively neutral flavour. Disease resistance cannot be translated directly into an aroma profile. Performance in Champagne requires assessment of blend proportions and ongoing trials; no fixed claims about aromas, acidity or ageing capacity are made without sufficient validation.
geneticsNote: Plantgrape identifies the parents as Villaris and a Muscadinia rotundifolia-derived selection, without giving the latter’s specific code. This entry retains that verified level of detail: it does not imply a direct cross with the wild species or guess a breeding code.
confusions: Not a Chardonnay mutation. Inclusion in Champagne trials does not make it an unconditionally authorized traditional variety. Col-2011G is a breeder’s reference code; Plantgrape lists no officially recognized varietal synonyms.

summary: A northern Greek red variety whose name refers to acidity and black colour, although its skins are not particularly deeply coloured. High acidity, firm tannins and savoury complexity support long ageing.
origin: A traditional variety of northern Greece.
viticulture: Sensitive to site and yield. Underripe fruit can show severe acidity and tannins; adequate ripeness must be achieved while retaining freshness.
winemaking: Used for varietal wines and local blends, as well as rosé and sparkling wines. Traditional dry reds often develop through oak and bottle ageing.
taste: Red fruit, tomato, olive, flowers and tobacco, with high acidity and firm tannins.
geneticsNote: The complete parentage has not been verified in this edition; hypotheses are not presented as established findings.
confusions: Comparisons with Nebbiolo describe stylistic similarities; they do not establish identity or a genetic relationship.

origin: A traditional Slovenian red; the celebrated old vine in Maribor is this variety, also used in Dolenjska’s Cviček blends.
summary: A late-ripening Slovenian red understood through both varietal wines and traditional red-white blends.
viticulture: Very late ripening, placed in the fourth ripening period, with potentially large bunches. Maribor’s old vine is a historical individual, not a general yield or vine-age model.
winemaking: Used in Cviček’s red-white blend and in light rosé examples. Steel vinification of the old-vine wine is a specific example, not a universal method.
taste: Can give light, low-alcohol styles. Cviček’s freshness and light body describe a blend and cannot be assigned entirely to one grape.

summary: Noted for gentle herbal aromas, freshness and local identity. Once almost confined to Vipava, it illustrates the preservation of distinctive varieties in a small region.
origin: An old local variety of the Vipava Valley; its name means “green”.
viticulture: Closely associated with Vipava’s opoka soils. No unverified disease-resistance traits or precise ripening periods are inferred here.
winemaking: Often vinified in stainless steel or concrete to retain freshness. Quality wines can also age and should not all be assumed to lack development potential.
taste: Dried Mediterranean herbs, light grassy notes, apricot and lemon, with a fresh, mildly aromatic profile.
geneticsNote: The sources reviewed for this entry do not establish both parents; no unverified parentage is supplied.
confusions: The name’s meaning does not indicate unripe grapes or an environmental winemaking certification. It is not a translated synonym of other varieties with “green” in their names.

summary: A pink-skinned white-wine variety of Thermenregion, notable for acidity and extract, bottled alone or with Rotgipfler.
origin: Probably originated in Austria’s Thermenregion. Spätrot is an important local name; Cirfandli is used in Hungary.
viticulture: Late budburst, mid-season flowering and mid-to-late ripening. Pink to grey-red ripe skins and compact bunches; tolerates drought and lime, but cropping and ripening can be uneven. Weak winter hardiness; Klosterneuburg rates downy-mildew and Botrytis tolerance poorly. It is not a disease-resistant cultivar.
winemaking: Vinified alone or with Rotgipfler; acidity and extract support structured white wines with ageing potential.
taste: Often restrained when young, with concentrated texture and marked acidity; honeyed notes may emerge with development.
geneticsNote: Roter Veltliner × an unidentified variety related to Traminer; the second parent is not established as Traminer itself.
confusions: Not Zinfandel. Spätrot-Rotgipfler denotes a blend of two varieties.

origin: An indigenous Herzegovinian white associated with the region’s karst vineyards.
summary: Usually a textured dry white, balancing alcohol, extract and acidity, with potential for bottle development.
viticulture: Suited to rocky sites with warm, dry summers; vigorous and upright, regularly productive, ripening slightly before Blatina.
winemaking: Bottled varietally or with small additions of Bena and Krkošija; a Žilavka label should not automatically be read as 100%.
taste: Yellow-green to gold, herbal or floral, with substantial body and extract; acidity balances the alcoholic weight.

confusions: Bena and Krkošija are companion or blending grapes, not synonyms of Žilavka or established parents.

summary: The same variety as Primitivo and Tribidrag. Climate, clonal selection and winemaking account for stylistic differences; the name alone does not determine a fixed taste profile.
origin: An ancient Croatian variety, subsequently developed through local selections and wine styles in the United States and Italy.
viticulture: Uneven ripening within bunches and berry shrivelling can produce high sugars. Harvest timing and sorting are important.
winemaking: Ranges from lighter to powerful dry reds, including old-vine field blends. White Zinfandel is a rosé style.
taste: Blackberry, raspberry, plum and pepper, with dried-fruit notes at greater ripeness. Warm-climate examples often have higher alcohol.
geneticsNote: Its genetic identity with Primitivo and Tribidrag is established, as is its status as a parent of Plavac Mali. Its own complete parentage is not presented here as definitively established.
confusions: White Zinfandel is not a white grape variety. Plavac Mali is an offspring, not a synonym.

summary: An Austrian red cross associated with fresh cherry fruit. It can be made for early drinking or as selected, concentrated wines with oak maturation.
origin: Bred in Klosterneuburg, Austria, in 1922.
viticulture: Productive, requiring crop and canopy management. Quality depends on balancing sugar, phenolic maturity and acidity, rather than colour alone.
winemaking: Used for varietal reds, blends and rosé. Stainless steel preserves fruit, while oak maturation can develop texture.
taste: Cherry, plum, berries and light spice, with fresh acidity. Tannins are often softer than those of ripe Blaufränkisch.
geneticsNote: St. Laurent × Blaufränkisch, bred by Fritz Zweigelt in 1922.
confusions: Rotburger should not be confused with the German variety Rotberger. Zweigelt is also distinct from Blauburger.
